lessons.plain: Overseeing a privacy and security plan means making sure the personal information an AI project uses is handled carefully from start to finish. Personal information, often called PII (personally identifiable information), is any data that can point to a specific person, such as a name, email address, or account number. A project manager does not write the encryption code, but must confirm that the rules exist, that someone is responsible for them, that only the right people can open the training data, and that a privacy impact assessment, a structured review of what personal data is collected, why, and what harm could result, was done before the model was built.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team wants to train a model on customer support chat logs that contain names and phone numbers. Before anyone writes code, what three things should you ask for, and why?
lessons.teach:
A privacy and security plan is the written set of rules that says what personal data an AI project may use, who may touch it, how it is protected, and how that protection is checked. Personal data, or PII (personally identifiable information), is any detail that can point to a specific person, alone or combined with other details. PII governance means the rules for finding it, labeling it, limiting it, and deciding who owns each decision.

Three controls do most of the work. Data minimization means collecting and keeping only the fields the model truly needs, because data you never stored cannot leak. Encryption protects data at rest, meaning stored on disk, and in transit, meaning moving over a network. A common pattern called envelope encryption locks each dataset with its own data key, and that data key is itself locked with a master key kept in a separate key service. Access controls, guided by least privilege, give each person and service only the permissions their job requires, and every access should be logged.

A privacy impact assessment (PIA) is a documented review, done before build work starts, that answers four questions: what personal data is involved, why it is needed, who could be harmed if it leaks or is misused, and which safeguards reduce that risk. The accountable owner signs off on the result.

Worked example: a team wants to train a churn model on call transcripts. Step 1: the PIA finds names and card numbers in the transcripts. Step 2: minimization removes the card numbers and replaces names with random IDs before training. Step 3: the remaining dataset is encrypted with its own data key, and only the two named data scientists and the training service account can read it. Step 4: the access log is reviewed monthly.

Common mistake: treating encryption as the whole plan. Encryption does not stop an authorized person from copying the data into a personal notebook, nor does it remove the need to ask whether the data should be used at all.

Consequence: if a copy of the training set lands on an unmanaged laptop, or a model memorizes and repeats a customer's phone number, the event is a reportable incident even though the storage was encrypted. Good oversight checks where copies live and what the model can reveal.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union trains a loan-default model on 40,000 applicant records. Step 1: the privacy impact assessment (PIA) lists full name, date of birth, and national ID number as personal data, and the accountable owner signs the PIA before build work starts. Step 2: data minimization drops the national ID and full date of birth, replaces the date of birth with an age band, and keeps only the income and repayment fields the model needs. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the model goes to production only after the credit union's privacy officer reviews the release. Which step belongs in the gap?
choices: Store the minimized dataset on a shared drive under one team password instead of encrypting it with its own data key and logging access.
Test the trained model by prompting it for applicant details and confirm it does not reproduce any name, ID, or account number from its training data.
Delete the access log after 30 days to reduce storage costs.
Give the external analytics vendor a full unmasked copy of the records so they can benchmark the model.
questions.why: A model can memorize and repeat personal details, so the gap needs a check for that before release, which is the consequence the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A team argues that its training file contains no personal data because every name has been removed. Which statement best corrects this reasoning?
choices: Removing names is always enough, because names are the only detail that identifies a person.
Any detail that can point to a specific person, alone or combined with other details, counts as PII, so removing names alone does not settle the question.
Personal data is only relevant once the file leaves the building, so the check can wait until export.
The team should count only fields marked as sensitive in the database schema, since those are the only fields that identify people.
questions.why: PII is defined by whether a detail can point to a person alone or in combination, so names are not the only identifier to check.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling model team wants to keep patient postcode as an input because it might improve predictions. Which response follows the minimization principle?
choices: Keep the postcode and list it as an accepted risk in the PIA so the owner can sign it off.
Keep the postcode, since storage is cheap and it might help later.
Keep the postcode but encrypt it, since encryption makes the field safe to hold.
Drop the postcode unless the model truly needs it, because data you never stored cannot leak.
questions.why: Minimization keeps only the fields the model truly needs, and a speculative benefit does not meet that test, so the field should be removed unless shown to be necessary.

questions.prompt: A customer service chatbot is trained on support chats. The team says its training storage was encrypted and only two engineers had read access, so no incident occurred after the bot repeated one customer's phone number to another user. What is the correct assessment?
choices: No incident occurred, because the data was never read by anyone unauthorized.
It is a reportable incident, because encryption at rest does not stop a model from memorizing and repeating personal data.
An incident may only be counted if the training file was downloaded to an outside device.
No incident occurred, because the phone number was only repeated by a bot.
questions.why: Encryption protects stored data but not what a trained model reveals, so the repeated phone number is a reportable incident regardless of storage protections.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a privacy impact assessment should happen before model training starts, and name one limit of encryption as a privacy control.
lessons.modelAnswer: A privacy impact assessment comes first because it decides whether personal data should be used at all, and which fields can be dropped, before effort and cost go into training. Once a model has learned from raw personal data, removing that data later is hard, and the model may have absorbed details that can resurface in its outputs. The assessment also names an accountable owner and the safeguards that must exist, such as minimization, access limits and logging, so the build team has clear requirements to meet. One limit of encryption is that it protects data from people outside the system, not from people inside it who already have access. An authorized analyst can still export, copy, or misuse the decrypted data, so encryption must be paired with access reviews, logging, and rules about where copies may live.
rubricPoints: Explains that the privacy impact assessment comes before build work so data use and minimization are decided early
Names an accountable owner and the safeguards the assessment requires
Describes encryption at rest and in transit together with least-privilege access
States that encryption does not stop authorized misuse or unmanaged copies

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which privacy safeguard a situation calls for adds the most, since no listed mission covers PII governance directly.

lessons.plain: Transparency in AI means being able to answer three questions clearly for the people who depend on a system: why the team picked this kind of model, where the training data came from, and how someone can understand why the system gave a particular answer. Think of it like a recipe card kept with a dish. It lists the ingredients, explains why the cook chose this method, and notes what to watch for if a guest has an allergy. A project manager makes sure this paperwork exists, stays current, and is written in language that sponsors, auditors, and frontline users can actually read.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's loan-approval model rejects an applicant, and the applicant asks why. Before anyone has explained anything, what three pieces of written information would you want the team to have ready, and why would each one matter?
lessons.teach:
A model-selection rationale is a written record of the candidate approaches the team considered, the criteria used to compare them (such as accuracy, speed, cost, and how easily the result can be explained), and the reason the chosen approach won. A data-source report is a record of each dataset the model learned from: where it came from, who owns it, when it was collected, what it covers, and what it leaves out. An explainability requirement is a stated, agreed expectation, set before the build, about how much the team must be able to explain a single prediction or the model's overall behaviour, and to whom. Why this works: a decision with no record cannot be reviewed later. A written rationale lets a reviewer test whether the choice still holds when data or constraints change.

Worked example. A subscription company builds a churn model. Step 1: the team compares a tree-based model, a simpler linear model, and a neural network. Step 2: the rationale notes the linear model is slightly less accurate, but its results can be explained to the retention team, which requires a reason for every flagged customer. That criterion is written down and signed off. Step 3: the data report lists billing data (exported monthly, owned by finance), support tickets (from 2022, chat excluded), and usage logs (sampled at 10 percent). Step 4: the explainability requirement says each flagged customer comes with its top three contributing factors. Step 5: six months later usage logging becomes complete. A reviewer sees that the sampling note is now wrong and updates the data report.

Common mistake: writing the documentation after release, or calling a choice industry standard without naming the alternatives and the criteria used to reject them.

Consequence in a running system: if a data source changes silently, predictions drift and nobody can tell whether the model or the data changed. The documentation is how the team finds out, and it is the first thing an auditor asks for.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain builds a model to forecast daily bread demand for each store. Step 1: the team compares a gradient-boosted tree model, a seasonal averaging method, and a deep neural network, using accuracy, cost, and speed as its criteria. Step 2: the seasonal averaging method is slightly less accurate, but its forecasts can be explained to store managers, who must justify each order to head office. The team writes this criterion down and gets sign-off. Step 3: the data report lists point-of-sale sales (owned by the operations team, collected since 2021, covering only the 40 stores with the new till system) and daily weather records from a public source. Step 4 is missing: the explainability requirement for this project has not yet been written. Step 5: after a year, two stores are removed from the sales feed, and nobody updates the data report. Which completion correctly fills in step 4?
choices: The model must reach 95 percent accuracy on a holdout set before any review takes place.
Explainability will be discussed with the managers once the bakery has opened a new store.
Store managers can view the sales table for their own store only.
Store managers receive the top three factors behind each order forecast, agreed and recorded before the build.
questions.why: An explainability requirement is an agreed expectation set before the build that states how much must be explained and to whom, and only the second choice states both the amount (top three factors) and the audience (store managers) before the build.

questions.prompt: A lending startup's data-source report for a credit-risk model says only 'customer data, 2020 onward.' Which addition best makes this a usable data-source report under the course definition?
choices: Source, owning team, collection dates, coverage, and known gaps.
A list of the data scientists who will maintain the model after launch.
A statement that the data meets industry standards.
The accuracy score of the model on its training data.
questions.why: A data-source report records where each dataset came from, who owns it, when it was collected, what it covers, and what it leaves out, which the second choice lists directly.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm chose a deep neural network for route-time prediction because it had the highest test accuracy. No other approaches were recorded, and the explanation dispatchers would need was left for later. Which description best names the problem?
choices: The team picked the wrong model, since a linear model would always have been better.
The explanation should have been written after release, once real results are known.
Accuracy is not a valid criterion for choosing a model at all.
No alternatives or criteria were recorded, so no reviewer can test whether the choice still holds.
questions.why: A model-selection rationale must name the candidates considered and the criteria used to compare and reject them, so its absence leaves the choice untestable, which the fourth choice identifies.

questions.prompt: A retail team's churn model began drifting after a data feed was changed without notice. Which question can the team's existing documentation most directly help them answer?
choices: Whether the model or the data changed, by comparing the documented data sources with the current feed.
Which vendor supplied the original training algorithm.
How many customers will churn next quarter.
Whether the retention team will accept the model going forward.
questions.why: Documented data sources let a team compare what the model was built on with what it is now receiving, which shows whether the data or the model is the source of the drift.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked on AI why a project manager should require a written model-selection rationale and a data-source report before a model goes live. Name one limit or tradeoff of documenting this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: The main reason is that a live model makes decisions about real people, and those decisions must be reviewable later. The model-selection rationale records which options we considered, the criteria we used, and why we chose this one, so that when someone asks why we did not use a simpler approach, we have an answer. The data-source report records where the training data came from, who owns it, what period it covers, and what is missing, so we can tell whether a change in the data explains a change in behaviour. The tradeoff is that this documentation takes real time, and it goes stale quickly if nobody maintains it. A rationale written once and never updated can mislead people more than no document at all, so the team needs a review step when data or requirements change.
rubricPoints: Names the model-selection rationale and what it records, such as alternatives considered and criteria used
Describes the data-source report: origin, ownership, coverage, and known gaps
Explains why these records let reviewers and auditors check decisions later
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as maintenance effort or stale documentation

suggested.rationale: Explaining the rationale and data records back to a teammate, including a limit, is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A bias check is a deliberate look at whether an AI system treats some groups of people worse than others, and why. Bias can come from the examples used to teach the system, from how the model was built, or from the decision rule that turns scores into yes or no answers. Project managers need to know which specific check to ask for, because a general promise to be fair cannot be tested. This lesson covers three common checks: looking at who is represented in the data, measuring outcomes for each group, and applying a fix when a gap appears.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI model that screens job applicants is 92 percent accurate overall. Before anyone looks at details, what is one reason that overall number alone might not show the model is fair to everyone?
lessons.teach: A bias check is a planned review that asks whether an AI system treats different groups of people unfairly. It can look at three places where unfairness enters: the data (the examples the model learned from), the model (how it was built and tuned), and the algorithm (the decision procedure that turns scores into outcomes, such as a score cutoff). Demographic representation analysis counts how many examples come from each group, such as age bands, regions or gender, and compares those shares with the population the system will actually serve. Fairness testing measures outcomes: for each group it computes a rate, such as the share of applicants approved, and compares the rates. A ratio of the lowest rate to the highest below about 0.8 (the four-fifths guideline used in some hiring settings) is a common warning sign. Bias-mitigation techniques are changes made after a gap is found: collecting more data for under-represented groups, reweighting training examples, adjusting thresholds where the law allows, or removing a feature that stands in for a protected trait. Worked example: a loan model is trained on past approvals, and one rural region makes up 8 percent of the training rows but 20 percent of customers. Step 1, representation analysis shows the gap. Step 2, fairness testing shows a 45 percent approval rate in that region versus 70 percent elsewhere, a ratio of about 0.64. Step 3, the team reweights the rural rows, retrains, and retests both the ratio and overall accuracy. Common mistake: checking only overall accuracy, which can look healthy while one group is served far worse. Consequence: in a live system a biased score quietly sends real customers toward rejection, so the bias check must be repeated whenever the data or the model changes.

questions.prompt: A regional college builds a model to shortlist scholarship applicants from past award decisions. First-generation students (the first in their family to attend college) are 35 percent of the applicant pool but only 12 percent of the training rows. Step 1: the representation analysis shows this gap. Step 2: fairness testing shows a shortlisting rate of 18 percent for first-generation applicants and 40 percent for everyone else. Step 3: the team divides 18 by 40 to get a ratio of 0.45, well below the 0.8 warning guideline. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the bias check correctly?
choices: Remove the score cutoff from the decision procedure so that every applicant is shortlisted regardless of score.
Report that overall accuracy rose to 91 percent, so the gap is acceptable and the check can close.
Delete every first-generation row from training so that the groups match, then retrain without them.
Reweight the first-generation training rows so they count in proportion to their share of the applicant pool, retrain, and retest both the ratio and overall accuracy.
questions.why: A mitigation such as reweighting is applied after a gap is found, and the correct action then retests both the group rate ratio and overall accuracy to confirm the gap closed without harm elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A streaming company's team reports that its recommendation model is fair because its overall accuracy is 93 percent. Which check would have exposed a problem that this single number hides?
choices: Comparing the model's accuracy against a model built last year
Checking that the model's code runs without errors on the test server
Counting the total number of users the model was trained on
Measuring the share of each user group that receives a recommendation and comparing those rates across groups
questions.why: Fairness testing measures outcome rates for each group and compares them, which can reveal unfairness that an overall accuracy figure conceals.

questions.prompt: A subscription company's churn model was trained on data where users from one region make up 6 percent of the rows, yet they make up 18 percent of the actual customer base the model will score. What is the first bias check step that addresses this?
choices: Run demographic representation analysis to compare each group's share of the training data with its share of the population served
Remove the region column and assume the gap disappears
Measure only the overall churn rate across the whole customer base
Adjust the decision threshold for every region upward by the same amount
questions.why: Representation analysis counts examples per group and compares those shares with the population the system serves, which is the step that reveals this under-representation.

questions.prompt: A housing-assistance team passed its bias check last quarter. This quarter it retrained its eligibility model on data from a newly added county. What should the team do about the bias check?
choices: Check only overall accuracy, because group rates are no longer relevant after a pass
Repeat the bias check, since both the data and the model have changed
Nothing, because a passed check remains valid for the life of the system
Wait for complaints from applicants before reviewing the model again
questions.why: A bias check must be repeated whenever the data or the model changes, because a new training set can introduce gaps that an earlier check would not have seen.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked with AI what a bias check on a loan-approval model involves, and name one limit or tradeoff of the fix you would recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: A bias check on a loan model has three parts. First, representation analysis: we count how many training records come from each region, age band or other group and compare that with the customers we actually serve. Second, fairness testing: we compare outcomes, such as approval rates, across those groups, and a ratio well below 0.8 is a warning sign that needs investigation. Third, mitigation: if a gap is confirmed, we might reweight or add data for under-represented groups, then retrain and retest. The tradeoff I would raise is that reweighting can lower overall accuracy or shift errors onto another group, so we must check the results for every group, not just the average. We also need to confirm with legal and compliance which adjustments are allowed, because some threshold changes by group may not be permitted.
rubricPoints: Describes checking representation in the data against the served population
Explains fairness testing by comparing outcome rates across groups
Names at least one mitigation technique such as reweighting or adding data
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as accuracy loss or shifted errors
Notes that legal or compliance review may constrain the fix

suggested.rationale: A bias question in an exam-style governance situation tests whether the learner picks the specific check that fits, which none of the current missions or planned engines exercise directly.

lessons.plain: Laws and company rules about AI keep changing, and an AI project has to follow whichever ones apply to it. Monitoring regulatory and policy compliance means keeping a running watch on those rules, working out which ones touch your project, and making sure the people who interpret them, the legal and compliance team, are involved early and often. Think of a shipping company that must track customs rules in every country it sends goods to. The rules change, and someone has to notice and tell the crew before a shipment gets stopped at the border. As a project manager, you are the link that turns outside rules into dated tasks and decisions.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team is building a model that scores job applicants. A new AI law has been announced in a region where you sell the product, but it is not yet in force. Who should hear about it first, and what should happen to the project plan before the law takes effect?
lessons.teach:
Regulatory compliance means meeting the legal rules that apply to a system. A policy is an internal rule your organization sets, such as a requirement to review every high-impact model before release. An obligation is a single specific duty that a rule places on you, such as telling people when an automated tool is used on them. Horizon scanning is the regular habit of looking for new or changing rules that may affect your project. A compliance register is a living list that records each obligation, the region or product it covers, who owns it, and the date it takes effect. The legal and compliance team are the people qualified to interpret what a rule means for your system; the project manager's job is to bring them the facts and turn their answers into work.

This works because rules differ by region and sector, they change over time, and missed obligations lead to fines, delays, or forced changes to a live product. A repeatable watch with a named owner prevents surprises.

Worked example: a hiring-screening model is used for applicants in two regions. Step 1: list the regions where applicants live. Step 2: for each, log the obligations in the register, such as notifying candidates that an automated tool is involved. Step 3: assign an owner from the legal team and a date for review. Step 4: when a new rule is announced, schedule a legal review, identify which features and screens it affects, and add tasks that must finish before its effective date.

Common mistake: treating compliance as a one-time sign-off at launch. The rules and the model's use both change, so the check must repeat.

Consequence: a model deployed without the required candidate notice may have to be pulled or retrofitted, which delays the release and the business value it was meant to deliver.

Compliance is an ongoing project activity, owned and tracked like any other risk.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uses an AI tool that ranks delivery drivers for shift allocation in three countries. In week one, the project manager records each country's obligations in the compliance register and names a legal owner for each. Three weeks later, one country announces a new rule requiring drivers to be told when a ranking affects their shifts, with an effective date 60 days away. The project manager sends the rule text to the legal team for interpretation and lists which driver app screens show shift rankings. The step still missing is: what should happen next so the change is actually built and ready in time?
choices: Ask the engineering lead to decide whether the rule applies, since they understand the model best.
Add tasks for the driver notice to the release plan, each with an owner and a completion date set before the 60-day effective date.
Set the register entry aside until the next annual review, because the legal interpretation is still pending.
Publish the notice as a footer on the driver app login page so every driver in all three countries sees it.
questions.why: Once legal has interpreted the rule, the project manager turns that answer into tracked work with owners and deadlines that finish before the effective date, which is the step the scenario leaves out.

questions.prompt: In a compliance register, what is an obligation?
choices: The regular habit of scanning for new or changing rules that might affect the project.
The legal team's written opinion on what a rule means for a particular system.
A single specific duty that a rule places on the team, such as telling people when an automated tool is used on them.
A internal rule the organisation sets for itself, such as requiring a review before every release.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an obligation as one specific duty a rule places on you, distinguishing it from an internal policy, horizon scanning, and legal interpretation.

questions.prompt: A team runs a compliance check only at launch and then stops. Six months later a new rule takes effect that the model breaks. Which description best captures the core problem?
choices: The legal team should have sent the rule to the project manager automatically.
Compliance was treated as a one-time sign-off, but rules and the model's use both change, so the check has to repeat.
The team chose a poor register format, so the rule was stored in the wrong place.
The team set the wrong effective date when the register was first created.
questions.why: The teaching text names treating compliance as a one-time launch sign-off as the common mistake, because both the rules and the system's use change over time.

questions.prompt: On an AI project, who is qualified to interpret what a new regulation means for the system, and what is the project manager's role?
choices: The project manager interprets the rule; the legal team only signs off on the final release.
The legal and compliance team interprets the rule; the project manager brings them the facts and turns their answers into work.
The regulator publishes a direct interpretation for each project, so no internal interpretation is needed.
The engineering team interprets the rule, because only they know how the model behaves.
questions.why: The teaching text states that the legal and compliance team interprets what a rule means for a system, while the project manager supplies facts and converts the answers into tasks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked with compliance how you would keep an AI project up to date with changing AI regulations, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on the legal team's interpretation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every region and sector where the system is used, then log each applicable rule as an obligation in a compliance register with an owner and an effective date. I would review that register on a fixed schedule and watch for announced changes, bringing each one to the legal and compliance team with the specific features it touches. Their interpretation becomes the basis for tasks, such as notices to users or documentation updates, that I track before the effective date. The main limit is timing: legal teams often need the system's actual behaviour described in plain facts before they can judge it, so a vague project description can delay the answer. Another tradeoff is that their advice is expert opinion rather than a guarantee, so the project still needs to re-check obligations when the model or its use changes.
rubricPoints: Identify the applicable regions and rules, and record obligations with owners and dates
Describe a repeating watch for new or changing regulations rather than a one-time check
Explain the project manager's role in bringing facts to legal and compliance and turning advice into tasks
Name a real limit, such as timing, the need for accurate system facts, or that legal advice is not a guarantee

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how to keep compliance current and naming its tradeoffs, which is best practised by talking it through rather than clicking through a mission.

lessons.plain: Accountability documentation and audit trails are the written and recorded evidence showing who built an AI system, what it was built from, and who approved it at each stage. Version control means saving each version of the model, the data it learned from, and the steps used to train it, so you can point to exactly which one was in use on a given day. An audit trail is a time-ordered record of changes and decisions that someone outside the project can check later. Think of it as a lab notebook that a regulator, a customer, or your own team can read months after the experiment ran.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a customer disputes a loan decision an AI model made last spring, what would you need on file to work out which model made it, what data trained it, and who signed off on releasing it?
lessons.teach:
Accountability documentation is the written record that answers who is responsible for each part of an AI system. An audit trail is a time-ordered log of changes and decisions that an independent reviewer can follow. Version control means keeping every saved version of three things: the model (the learned parameters and the code that produces them), the data (training and test sets, captured as snapshots with fixed identifiers), and the training process (code commit, settings such as learning rate and random seed, and the environment). A stakeholder approval record is a dated entry showing that a named person with authority, such as a product owner, risk lead, or compliance reviewer, reviewed a specific version and accepted or rejected it.

Why it works: a model can only be explained or reproduced if you can rebuild it from the same inputs. Tying each model version to a data snapshot ID, a code commit, and a settings file lets anyone rerun training and compare results. Tying each version to an approval record shows that a human accepted that exact version before it reached users.

Worked example: a team retrains a churn model in March. They record model version 3.1, the training data snapshot ID for 28 February, code commit 4f2a, the settings file, and the accuracy and fairness metrics. The product owner and privacy reviewer each sign an approval entry naming version 3.1 and the date. In June, a prediction is questioned. The team looks up the model version used for that prediction, finds 3.1, finds its data snapshot, and confirms the approval record exists.

Common mistake: saving only the model file. Without the data snapshot and training code, the team cannot explain how the file was made, and the approval may refer to something that can no longer be rebuilt.

Consequence: in a live system, a rollback or dispute requires knowing which version is serving traffic and what it was trained on. Missing records mean the team cannot safely roll back or answer an auditor, and every version needs a named owner and approver.

questions.prompt: Priya's team at a regional insurer releases claims-triage model v2.4 on 9 May. They save the model parameters as v2.4, record training data snapshot ID CL-0412 (data cut 31 March), code commit 9bc0, and a settings file with random seed 42. Before release, the claims director and a fairness analyst each sign a dated approval entry naming v2.4. In August, a triage decision is disputed. Step 1: the team looks up which model version served that decision and finds v2.4. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the team confirms that the signed approval entries for v2.4 exist.
choices: Replace v2.4 with the newest version so the disputed decision is no longer served to anyone.
Delete the two approval entries and sign new ones so they match the model that is serving now.
Retrieve snapshot CL-0412, commit 9bc0 and the seed-42 settings file so the v2.4 training run can be rebuilt and checked.
Retrain the model on the latest August claims so the disputed decision reflects current behaviour.
questions.why: Rebuilding the version from its recorded snapshot, commit and settings is what lets the team reproduce and explain the exact model that made the disputed decision.

questions.prompt: Under the course's definition, which set of items makes up the version record of the training process?
choices: The model parameters and the approval entries that name them
The code commit, the settings such as learning rate and random seed, and the environment
The data snapshot IDs and the dates they were captured
The accuracy and fairness metrics reported for the release
questions.why: The teaching text defines the training process version as the code commit, the settings such as learning rate and random seed, and the environment.

questions.prompt: A team keeps every model file and every signed approval entry, but deletes the training data snapshots after 90 days to save storage. What is the main risk?
choices: Auditors will stop accepting the model file as a valid version.
An approval may refer to a version that can no longer be rebuilt, so the team cannot explain how it was made.
The approval records become invalid because they no longer list a data snapshot.
The model will stop serving predictions once its data is removed.
questions.why: Without the snapshot and training code, the approved version cannot be reproduced, so the team cannot explain it or answer a dispute about it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid stakeholder approval record under the course's definition?
choices: A dated entry in which a named risk lead records that they reviewed model version 5.0 and accepted it.
A chat message from a developer saying looks good, sent before the final model was trained.
A wiki page listing the names of everyone on the project, without linking any approval to a version.
A meeting note saying the team agreed the model is ready, with no version number or date.
questions.why: A valid approval record is dated, names a person with authority, and shows that person reviewed and accepted or rejected a specific version.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has not worked on AI governance what a model version, a data snapshot, and an approval record each contribute to an audit trail, and name one limit of keeping these records.
lessons.modelAnswer: A model version is a saved, numbered copy of the trained model, but on its own it only shows what the model is, not how it was made. A data snapshot is a frozen copy of the training data with a fixed ID, so the team can say exactly which examples taught it. An approval record is a dated entry showing a named stakeholder reviewed that specific version and accepted it. Together they form an audit trail: from any live prediction you can go back to the version, the data, and the person who signed off. The limit is that the records only help if they are complete and tied to exact versions. A snapshot saved without the code commit, or an approval for version 3.0 quietly reused for 3.1, looks like traceability but cannot be reproduced. Also, the trail shows what was decided, not whether the decision was fair; that still needs separate bias and explainability checks.
rubricPoints: Defines model version, data snapshot, and approval record in plain terms.
Explains that together they let you trace a live prediction back to its version, its data, and its approver.
States a limit: records must be complete and tied to exact versions, or the traceability is false.
Notes that an audit trail shows decisions, not fairness, so separate checks are still needed.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how version and approval records link together, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this governance practice.

lessons.plain: Before anyone builds an AI tool, someone has to say clearly what problem it is meant to solve and for whom. Identifying the problem means describing the people who will use or be affected by a solution, using short written profiles called user personas that capture a typical user's goals and frustrations. It also means turning a business pain into a question that a type of AI can answer, then checking that wording with subject matter experts, the people who really do the work day to day. If this step is skipped, a team can build something technically impressive that nobody needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A call-centre manager says her team needs an AI tool that makes agents faster. Before anyone chooses a technology, what two questions would you ask her, and why might her answers matter more than which model you pick?
lessons.teach:
A user persona is a short, specific profile of one type of person who will use the solution, including their daily tasks, goals, and pain points. A problem statement is a one or two sentence description of a business problem that names the current pain, who feels it, and what a good outcome looks like. An AI pattern is a general type of task that AI can perform, such as classification (sorting items into fixed labels), prediction (estimating a number or a future value), ranking (ordering items by relevance), anomaly detection (flagging unusual cases), or generation (producing new text or images). A subject matter expert, or SME, is someone with deep hands-on knowledge of the work.

Why this works: a pattern can only be chosen once the problem is precise. Consider a returns team that spends hours deciding whether damage claims are covered. Step one: the persona is a returns clerk who handles about 80 claims a day. Step two: the problem statement reads, clerks spend about six minutes per claim deciding coverage, and we need to cut that without more wrong approvals. Step three: choosing one label from a fixed set of options is classification. Step four: senior clerks review the statement and reveal that the real delay is missing purchase dates, not judging photos. The problem is restated before any data is collected.

The common mistake is starting from the tool, such as we want a chatbot, and working backwards to a problem. Consequence in a running system: the team collects photos, builds a model that scores well on its own metrics, and users quietly ignore it because it never removed the real bottleneck.

A precise, SME-validated problem statement is the foundation every later feasibility and ROI decision depends on.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility's customer service team has three billing reps, each handling about 60 calls a day. Step one: the persona is a billing rep who must explain to a customer why a bill jumped. Step two: the problem statement reads, reps spend about five minutes per call finding why a bill jumped, and we need to cut that without giving customers wrong explanations. Step three: the team picks a pattern for sorting each high-bill case into one of six fixed causes such as a leak, a meter fault, a tariff change, or an estimated reading, which is classification. Step four is missing: before any data is collected, the team sits down with two senior reps to test the problem statement. What should that step accomplish?
choices: Pick the largest available model so the classifier reaches high accuracy.
Check the problem statement with the reps and restate it before collecting data.
Have the reps draft a chatbot script so the tool is chosen first.
Count the total number of calls per year to set the project budget.
questions.why: Validating the problem statement with SMEs before data collection is what can reveal the real bottleneck and restate the problem precisely.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy wants software that estimates how many units of a common blood-pressure medicine will be dispensed next week. Which AI pattern fits this need?
choices: Prediction, because the system must estimate a number for a future value
Anomaly detection, because the system must flag unusual dispensing
Classification, because each week is sorted into a fixed label
Generation, because the system must produce new text describing demand
questions.why: Estimating a number for a future value is the definition of prediction, while the other patterns sort, order, flag unusual cases, or create new content.

questions.prompt: A product team proposes building a chatbot for field technicians. They have not yet named who the technicians are, what their daily tasks are, or what a good outcome looks like. Which mistake is the team making?
choices: Choosing ranking because it sounds more advanced than classification in a meeting
Writing the persona after the model has already been trained and tested
Asking SMEs to rate the model's accuracy before the problem is defined
Starting from the tool and working backwards to a problem
questions.why: Starting from a tool and working backwards to a problem is the common mistake the teaching text describes, because the problem has not been made precise.

questions.prompt: A bank's loan officers receive a large daily queue of applications. The team wants the system to order the queue so the applications most likely to be complete and ready for decision appear first. Which AI pattern matches this need?
choices: Classification, because each application is sorted into a fixed label
Generation, because the system produces new summaries of each file
Anomaly detection, because the system flags unusual applications
Ranking, because items are ordered by relevance or priority
questions.why: Ordering items by relevance or priority is ranking, and the other patterns sort into labels, flag unusual cases, or create new content, none of which describes the requested queue order.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we write a user persona and validate the problem statement with subject matter experts before choosing an AI approach. Name one limit or tradeoff of this step.
lessons.modelAnswer: We write the persona so the team knows exactly who the solution is for, what their day looks like, and what they would need to change to adopt it. The problem statement then turns a vague complaint into something measurable, with a current pain and a target outcome. Only then can we map it to an AI pattern: if the output is one choice from a fixed set, that points to classification; if it is a number, prediction; if it is ordering items, ranking. Validating with SMEs matters because managers often describe symptoms, while the people doing the work know the actual bottleneck. The tradeoff is time and access: SME sessions take their hours away from operations, and personas can drift into stereotypes if they are written from assumptions rather than observation. We mitigate that by naming the sources for each persona and revisiting the statement after the first pilot.
rubricPoints: A persona describes a specific user, their goals, and their pain points, not a generic user
A good problem statement names the current pain, who feels it, and a measurable target
The problem is mapped to an AI pattern such as classification, prediction, ranking, or generation based on the output needed
SMEs check the statement against how the work really happens, and a limit or tradeoff is named

suggested.rationale: This objective is mainly tested by explaining a problem framing back in your own words, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Before anyone builds an AI system, a project manager checks whether it is worth trying at all. Initial feasibility means asking four plain questions: can the technology actually do this job, is there enough usable data about the problem, does the team have the computing power and budget to run it, and is the organization ready to use the result. A feasibility check does not prove the project will succeed. It finds the reasons it could fail early, while those reasons are still cheap to fix. Think of it like inspecting a house before buying it: you look at the structure, the wiring, the water supply, and whether you can actually move in before you sign anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team wants an AI tool that drafts replies to customer tickets using past replies. Before anyone picks a model, what is the first thing you would check, and why would you check it first?
lessons.teach:
Initial AI feasibility is a structured check, done before significant build work, of four things. Technical viability asks whether the chosen kind of AI can plausibly solve the problem at the needed accuracy. Data availability asks whether the data needed to learn and test the system exists and can legally and practically be accessed. Data quality asks whether that data is complete, consistent, labelled correctly, and representative of the cases the system will face. Computational resource requirements are the processors, memory, storage, and recurring cost needed to train and run the system. Organizational readiness asks whether people, processes, skills, and sponsorship exist to act on what the system produces.

Worked example: a fleet operator proposes predicting which delivery vans will need unplanned maintenance within 14 days. Step 1, technical viability: predicting failures from sensor history is a established pattern, so the approach is plausible. Step 2, data: three years of telemetry exist, but failure records live in paper workshop logs for only about 40 percent of vans. That is a quality gap. Step 3, compute: retraining nightly on about two million rows fits a modest server, so cost is low. Step 4, readiness: planners have no process for acting on a risk score. Verdict: not yet feasible. Digitize the failure records and agree a planner workflow, then run a small pilot.

Common mistake: treating feasibility as a single accuracy question, or assuming data exists because it was collected somewhere. The consequence in a running system is serious. A model trained on incomplete failure labels learns that vans with no records never fail, so it produces confident alerts that are wrong, and planners who were never prepared to act simply stop trusting it.

A feasibility check ends in a documented verdict on each of the four areas, with the blockers named and the conditions for proceeding stated.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer wants to flag motor claims that may be fraudulent before payout. Step 1, technical viability: flagging suspicious claims from past claim features is a well-understood classification approach, so it is plausible. Step 2, data: six years of claim records exist and can be accessed, but fraud labels exist only for the roughly 8 percent of claims that were sent to investigators, so the labels cover mainly suspicious cases. Step 4, readiness: claims handlers have agreed to send flagged claims to a named review queue with a two-day turnaround. Step 3, compute, is not yet recorded. The facts gathered for it are: retraining monthly on about 40 million rows, one 16 GB laptop as the only machine, and no agreed budget for storage or recurring cloud cost. Which Step 3 entry should be recorded?
choices: Compute is adequate, because a laptop can train any classification model given enough time.
Compute is judged by the model's accuracy on the test set, so it cannot be assessed until the build is complete.
Compute is a blocker to be sized: the team must cost the processors, memory, storage, and recurring cost to train and run the system at 40 million rows before proceeding.
Compute is not a feasibility item, so it can be left to the engineering team after the pilot.
questions.why: Computational resource requirements cover processors, memory, storage, and recurring cost for both training and running the system, and the gathered facts show these are unsized and unfunded, so they must be named as a blocker with a condition for proceeding.

questions.prompt: In a feasibility check, which question does organizational readiness ask?
choices: Whether the processors, memory, and storage needed to train the system are affordable.
Whether the data needed to learn and test the system can be legally accessed.
Whether the chosen kind of AI can reach the needed accuracy on the problem.
Whether people, processes, skills, and sponsorship exist to act on what the system produces.
questions.why: Organizational readiness is defined in the teaching text as whether people, processes, skills, and sponsorship exist to act on the system's output, which is different from the technical, data, and compute questions.

questions.prompt: A team reports that its model reached 95 percent accuracy on the data it was built with and concludes that the feasibility check is complete. Which is the most important gap in that conclusion?
choices: The team has not asked the sponsor to approve the accuracy target, which is a compute question.
The team has not confirmed the model is a deep neural network, which is required for feasibility.
The team has treated feasibility as a single accuracy question and has not checked whether its data is complete, consistent, correctly labelled, and representative of real cases.
The team has not measured how long the model takes to train, which is a readiness question.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that feasibility is not a single accuracy question, and that data quality, including whether the data represents the cases the system will face, must be checked separately.

questions.prompt: A bank has five years of customer chat transcripts that it wants to use to train a support assistant. The transcripts are stored and the bank's engineers can read them, but the privacy terms of the original collection do not permit using them to train new systems. Under the feasibility check, which area does this fact most directly fail?
choices: Organizational readiness, because the support staff have not agreed to use the assistant.
Technical viability, because chat assistants are not an established pattern.
Data availability, because the data cannot be legally accessed for the purpose of learning.
Computational resource requirements, because storing the transcripts is expensive.
questions.why: Data availability asks whether the data needed to learn and test the system exists and can legally and practically be accessed, and the transcripts exist but the terms forbid this use; the question's listed answer should be read as the one that matches this check, so the correct option is the one naming data availability.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would judge whether a proposed AI initiative is feasible before funding a build, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing this check early.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would go through four areas and record a finding for each. First, technical viability: is the kind of AI being proposed able to solve this problem, given what research and similar systems show? Second, data: do we have the records needed to learn and test, and are they complete, labelled correctly, and representative? Third, compute: what hardware, storage, and recurring cost would training and running it need, and does that fit the budget? Fourth, readiness: who will act on the output, is there a process for it, and does the sponsor have the skills and time? Each area gets a verdict of ready, conditional, or blocked, with the conditions written down. The limit is that an early check relies on assumptions that are only partly tested, so a feasible verdict is a reason to pilot, not a guarantee. It also takes effort before anyone has seen results, so it should be proportionate to the size of the investment.
rubricPoints: Covers all four areas: technical viability, data availability and quality, compute needs, and organizational readiness
Gives a clear verdict or condition for each area rather than a single overall opinion
Names a limit: early checks rest on untested assumptions and feasible does not mean successful
Notes that the check should be proportionate to the investment and followed by a small pilot

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style initiative with blockers in several areas adds the most, and no listed mission or planned engine covers feasibility judgement directly.

lessons.plain: Before a team builds an AI system, they ask what could go wrong and how badly it would hurt. A risk assessment lists the ways the system could fail, the ways someone could attack or misuse it, and the ways it could harm people or breach expectations of fairness and privacy. For each risk, the team estimates how likely it is and how severe it would be, then chooses a response: remove it, reduce it, monitor it, or accept it. Think of a building inspector walking the site before construction starts, checking the structure, the wiring, and the locks, not just whether the drawings look good. Done early, this shapes the design. Done late, it becomes an expensive surprise.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants an AI chatbot that answers customer questions using each customer's order history. Name two ways it could cause harm even if its answers are mostly accurate.
lessons.teach:
A failure mode is a specific way a system can stop doing its job or do it wrongly, such as a model that slowly becomes less accurate as customer behaviour changes. A cybersecurity vulnerability is a weakness someone can exploit, such as an unprotected API, a leaked credential, or a prompt injection, where crafted text tricks a language model into ignoring its rules. A safety risk is potential physical or financial harm to people from the system's outputs or actions. An ethics risk is an unfair outcome across groups, privacy exposure, or a decision nobody can explain. A mitigation is a control that lowers the likelihood or the impact of a risk. Residual risk is what remains after mitigation.

Worked example: a model pre-screens loan applications. Step 1: list failure modes. Applicant mix shifts, so accuracy drops; training data under-represents some regions. Step 2: list vulnerabilities. The scoring endpoint has no authentication, so anyone can probe it to learn the decision rule. Step 3: note safety and ethics risks. A wrong denial harms a family, and error rates may differ across groups. Step 4: score each risk as likelihood times impact on a one-to-five scale; the drift risk scores 3 by 4, which is 12. Step 5: choose mitigations: require authentication and rate limits, monitor error rates by group, and send every denial to a human reviewer. Step 6: record the residual risk and name an owner.

A common mistake is treating the assessment as a one-time document signed at kickoff, or listing only technical failures while ignoring misuse and ethics. In a running system, a model that degrades silently for six months causes wrong decisions at scale, and an unauthenticated endpoint lets outsiders copy the model.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union uses a model to flag card transactions for fraud review. Risk A: the model misses new fraud patterns after customer spending shifts. Likelihood 4, impact 3, score 12. Mitigation: retrain monthly on the last 90 days and alert the team weekly if the flag rate moves more than 20 percent. The team estimates this lowers likelihood to 2 and leaves impact at 3, so Risk A's residual risk is 2 times 3, which is 6. Risk B: the flagging endpoint accepts requests from any internal service account with no audit log, so someone holding one stolen credential could learn which transactions get flagged. Likelihood 3, impact 4, score 12. Mitigation: require per-service authentication and audit logging, which the team estimates lowers likelihood to 1 and leaves impact at 4. Missing step: compute the residual risk for Risk B using the post-mitigation likelihood and impact.
choices: 4, which is likelihood 1 times impact 4 after mitigation
3, which is the original likelihood alone
12, because mitigation leaves the original score unchanged
1, which is the post-mitigation likelihood alone
questions.why: Residual risk is recomputed as likelihood times impact using the values after the mitigation is applied, so 1 times 4 gives 4.

questions.prompt: A marketing team's shopping chatbot can be manipulated by a customer who types a message instructing it to reveal internal discount rules and ignore its guidelines. Which term best names this weakness?
choices: Mitigation
Cybersecurity vulnerability
Failure mode
Residual risk
questions.why: A cybersecurity vulnerability is a weakness someone can exploit, and crafted text that tricks a language model into ignoring its rules is a prompt injection, which is that kind of weakness.

questions.prompt: A hiring-screen model has an unexplained-rejection risk scored at likelihood 2 and impact 5. The team adds human review of every rejection, which they estimate keeps likelihood at 2 and lowers impact to 2. What is the residual risk, and what does the team still need to record?
choices: 7, which is the sum of likelihood and the new impact, and no owner is needed
2, which is the likelihood alone, and the original score of 10 should be deleted
10, and nothing else needs recording because the score is already known
4, which is 2 times 2 after mitigation, plus a named owner for that residual risk
questions.why: Residual risk is what remains after mitigation, so it is recalculated as likelihood times impact with the post-mitigation values (2 times 2 = 4), and the assessment should name an owner for it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's risk assessment for a delivery-routing model lists only the risk that route accuracy drops as traffic patterns change. A reviewer asks what is missing. Which answer is most accurate?
choices: A residual risk figure, because the assessment has not yet been mitigated
Nothing is missing, because drift is the only failure a routing model can have
Cybersecurity vulnerabilities and misuse, such as an exposed routing endpoint or a dispatcher credential that can be leaked
A named owner, because owners are only needed for ethics risks
questions.why: A thorough assessment covers vulnerabilities and misuse as well as technical failure modes, so an exposed endpoint or leaked credential is a gap a reviewer should raise.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would run a risk assessment for a proposed AI feature. Name the main risk categories, how you would rank the risks, and one tradeoff that a mitigation creates.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the ways the feature could fail: data drift, poor performance for certain user groups, and wrong outputs that people act on. Then I would check for security weaknesses, such as an open endpoint, leaked credentials, or inputs that could manipulate the model, and for safety and ethics issues like privacy exposure or unfair treatment. For ranking, I score each risk by likelihood and impact on a simple scale, and I focus first on the high-scoring ones. For each one, I pick a response: remove it, reduce it, monitor it, or accept it with an owner. A tradeoff I would flag is human review. It lowers the chance of a harmful automated decision, but it slows responses and adds staffing cost, so the team has to decide where review is worth that price. I would also name the residual risk I was accepting, so leadership makes that call knowingly.
rubricPoints: Names the main categories: failure modes, security vulnerabilities, safety, and ethics
Explains ranking risks by likelihood and impact before choosing responses
Gives a clear mitigation response for at least one risk
Identifies a real tradeoff a mitigation creates, such as cost, speed, or user experience
Mentions residual risk and assigning an owner

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario to choose the right risk technique and mitigation adds more than reading alone, and no existing mission or planned engine covers AI risk assessment directly.

lessons.plain: A project scope statement is a short written agreement that says what an AI project will and will not do, how anyone will know it has succeeded, and where its edges sit. Think of a moving company's written quote: it lists the boxes included, excludes jobs like moving a piano, and states when the job counts as finished. AI projects need this more than most, because a model can always be made a little better, and without written limits the team keeps adding features. Writing scope down before building lets people disagree early, when changing the plan is cheap.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI team is asked to 'build a churn predictor for our customers.' Before reading any further, list three things you would want written down before work starts, and say which one you would most worry about being missing.
lessons.teach:
A scope statement is a document that fixes the boundaries of an initiative. Its boundaries are the limits on what the project covers: which data sources it uses, which users it serves, which regions or product lines it touches, and which decisions the system informs. In-scope functionality is the list of capabilities the project will deliver. Out-of-scope functionality is the list of capabilities it explicitly will not deliver, including tempting ones. Success criteria are the measurable conditions that define done, such as a target result on recent data that was held back from training, agreed with the people who will use the output.

The reason this works is that AI work has no natural finish line. A written boundary turns 'make it better' into a fixed set of deliverables, and gives later change requests something concrete to be measured against.

Worked example. A dispatch team proposes 'predict arrival times for all depots.' The scope statement narrows it. Step one: the boundary is two pilot depots and twelve months of trip logs. Step two: in scope is an arrival estimate shown on the existing dispatcher screen. Step three: out of scope is automatic rerouting, customer text notifications, and other regions. Step four: the success criterion is an agreed error limit on the most recent two months of trips, plus dispatchers using the estimate during the pilot. When someone later asks for customer texts, the team records it as out of scope and opens a change request.

A common mistake is writing the out-of-scope list as 'everything else' or writing success as 'good accuracy.' Neither can be checked. The consequence in a running system is scope creep: the team quietly builds rerouting, the pilot slips, data pipelines the plan never funded appear, and nobody can say whether the model is finished.

questions.prompt: A regional medical-supply distributor is scoping a reorder forecast for one warehouse, the Harbor Street site. The scope statement so far reads as follows. Step one: the boundary is the Harbor Street warehouse and 18 months of its order records. Step two: in scope is a weekly reorder suggestion shown on the clerks' existing ordering screen. Step three: out of scope is supplier price negotiation and direct deliveries to hospitals. Step four is missing. Which completion finishes the scope statement correctly?
choices: The forecast runs nightly on the warehouse's own server
All other distribution centers are listed as out of scope
The clerks feel the forecast is accurate enough to trust
An agreed error limit on the latest two months of orders, held back from training
questions.why: The missing step is the success criterion, which must be a measurable condition checked on recent data held back from training and agreed with the users, and only the third choice does that.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud-alert team wants a success criterion for its scope statement. Which of these is one?
choices: The alert model has strong overall performance over time
The model runs on the bank's cloud account and not on-site
Every fraud type the bank has ever recorded is covered
Analysts confirm at least 80% of flags on last month's transactions, held out from training
questions.why: A success criterion must be a measurable condition, and only the second choice gives a specific threshold checked on recent held-back data that the users agreed to.

questions.prompt: Mid-pilot, a logistics firm's manager asks the AI team to add automatic invoice payment, which the scope statement lists as out of scope. What should the team do under its scope statement?
choices: Delete it from the out-of-scope list and build it
Record it as out of scope and open a change request
Treat it as new in-scope work without any review
Quietly add it, since it looks like a small change
questions.why: A written out-of-scope item is kept as it is, and any request to add it goes through a change request so the team can measure it against the agreed boundary.

questions.prompt: A clinic network's AI scope statement lists four items. Which one is a boundary, meaning a limit on data sources, users, regions, or decisions, rather than a capability to deliver?
choices: Shows a denial-risk score on the claims adjuster's screen
Sends automatic appeal letters to every patient in the county
Only claims records from two clinics, 2021 to 2023
Achieves an acceptable level of accuracy
questions.why: Limiting the project to specific claims records from two clinics and a set date range is a boundary on data sources, while the other choices describe deliverables or a vague goal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why an AI project scope statement needs an explicit out-of-scope list, and name one limit or tradeoff of writing scope too tightly early in a project.
lessons.modelAnswer: An explicit out-of-scope list matters because AI projects attract requests that sound small but change the work: a new data source, a new user group, an automatic action where there was only a recommendation. If those items are not named as excluded, they arrive as assumed work, and the schedule and budget stop matching the plan. Writing them down gives the team a clear answer and a path, such as a change request with its own estimate. The tradeoff is that a very tight scope made early can lock in assumptions that turn out wrong once real data is seen. So the scope statement should name what is excluded and also how it will be revisited, for example at a defined checkpoint after the pilot data is reviewed. The goal is boundaries that are firm enough to protect the schedule but explicit enough that changing them is a deliberate decision rather than drift.
rubricPoints: Out-of-scope items prevent unplanned work from arriving as assumed work.
Explicit boundaries let change requests be judged against a written baseline.
Writing scope too tightly early can lock in assumptions that real data later contradicts.
A good scope statement names a checkpoint or process for revisiting the boundaries.

suggested.rationale: Sorting realistic requests into in-scope, out-of-scope, and change-request buckets in an exam-style scenario adds the most, since no listed OpsForge mission or planned engine targets scope writing directly.

lessons.plain: When someone proposes an AI project, the central question is whether it is worth the money and effort. This objective is about answering that with numbers that decision-makers can trust. You estimate the value the project should produce, add up everything it will cost across its whole working life, and compare the two over a fixed period. That comparison is a cost-benefit analysis, and it usually reports a return on investment, which shows how much value comes back for each unit of money spent. A good analysis is honest about the running costs that a build estimate hides and about how uncertain the benefit numbers are.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team says their AI tool will save 2,000 staff hours a year and cost 100,000 to build. Name two things you would want to know before deciding whether the project is worth doing.
lessons.teach:
Return on investment (ROI) compares what a project gains with what it costs. For an AI initiative you need three pieces. Expected benefits are the measurable value you forecast, such as staff hours saved multiplied by a loaded rate (the full hourly cost of an employee, including overheads), or losses avoided. Total cost of ownership (TCO) is every cost across the whole life of the system, not just the build: data preparation, computing for training and for running predictions, software licences, monitoring, periodic retraining, the people who maintain it, and change management. A cost-benefit analysis sets benefits and costs side by side over a stated time horizon so stakeholders can decide whether to proceed. A common formula is (total benefits minus TCO) divided by TCO.

Why it works: AI systems carry recurring costs that a single build estimate hides, so comparing forecast benefits with full lifetime cost keeps the decision honest.

Worked example. A support team handles 20,000 tickets a year. An AI triage model is expected to save 1.5 minutes per ticket, which is 500 hours a year, or 30,000 a year at a loaded rate of 60 per hour. Step one: adjust for adoption. Only 60 percent of agents are expected to use the tool, so the realistic benefit is 18,000 a year. Step two: total the cost. The build is 80,000 once, and running costs are 40,000 a year for compute, licences, monitoring and retraining. Step three: over three years, benefits are 54,000 and TCO is 80,000 plus 120,000, or 200,000. ROI is (54,000 minus 200,000) divided by 200,000, about minus 73 percent. The case does not pay back in this horizon, so the team must cut run costs, raise adoption, or reject it.

Common mistake: treating the build cost as the total cost and the gross benefit as the return. This makes almost any project look profitable.

Consequence in a running system: if retraining is dropped to save money, model accuracy drifts, adoption falls, and the benefit assumed in the case quietly disappears while the costs continue.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer screens 12,000 claims a year for likely duplicates. Each check takes a reviewer 4 minutes, and the tool is expected to remove that check, valued at a loaded rate of 45 per hour (the full hourly cost of an employee, overheads included). Step one: the gross saving is 800 hours, or 36,000 a year. Step two: only 75 percent of reviewers are expected to use the tool, so the realistic annual benefit is 27,000. Step three: the build costs 60,000 once and running costs are 25,000 a year. Over a three-year horizon, the adjusted benefits total 81,000. Missing step: work out the three-year total cost of ownership (TCO, every cost over the system's whole life) and then the ROI using the standard formula, (total benefits minus TCO) divided by TCO. What is the ROI?
choices: About minus 40 percent, with a three-year TCO of 135,000
About minus 67 percent, dividing by the benefits instead of the TCO
About minus 20 percent, using unadjusted gross benefits
About plus 35 percent, using the build cost alone as TCO
questions.why: The three-year TCO is 60,000 plus three years of 25,000, which is 135,000, and (81,000 minus 135,000) divided by 135,000 is minus 40 percent.

questions.prompt: A team plans a two-year horizon for a document summary tool. The build costs 30,000 once, and running costs (licences, compute and monitoring together) are 16,000 a year. What is the total cost of ownership over the two years?
questions.why: TCO covers the build plus two years of running costs, so 30,000 plus 2 times 16,000 equals 62,000; the other figures use one year, or three years, of running costs.

questions.prompt: A manager argues a project is clearly worth funding because its gross benefits over three years, 120,000, are more than double its 50,000 build cost. What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
choices: The benefits should be divided by the build cost instead of subtracted from it
The three-year horizon is too short to compare benefits with anything
Nothing is wrong, because gross benefits above build cost always show a positive return
It leaves out running costs and adoption, so neither the TCO nor the adjusted benefits are counted
questions.why: Comparing gross benefits with only the build cost ignores the recurring costs of the system and the share of users who will actually adopt it, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A project has adjusted benefits of 90,000 over a two-year horizon and a TCO of 100,000. Under a standard cost-benefit analysis, what is the correct decision point?
choices: Yes, because the build cost is the only figure a stakeholder needs to see
Cannot be judged, since a cost-benefit analysis requires a horizon of at least five years before any ROI figure can be stated
Yes, because benefits are close enough to cost that the case pays back quickly
Not yet: ROI is about minus 10 percent over this horizon, so the case does not pay back and assumptions must change
questions.why: ROI is (90,000 minus 100,000) divided by 100,000, which is minus 10 percent, so the case does not pay back in the stated horizon and the team must cut run costs, raise adoption, or reject it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a proposed AI project is worth funding, and name one limit or tradeoff of the ROI figure you would present.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by forecasting the benefits in money terms, such as hours saved multiplied by a loaded hourly rate, and then reduce that figure for the share of users who will realistically adopt the tool. Next I would add up the total cost of ownership over the chosen time horizon, including build, data work, compute for training and predictions, licences, monitoring, retraining, and change management, not only the build. I would then compare the two and show ROI with the assumptions visible. The main limit is that the ROI figure depends heavily on the estimated adoption rate and the time horizon, so a small change in either can flip the answer. I would therefore show a range of scenarios and say which assumptions the decision rests on.
rubricPoints: Benefits are forecast in money terms and adjusted for realistic adoption
Total cost of ownership covers the whole lifecycle, not just the build
Benefits and costs are compared over a stated time horizon
The result is sensitive to assumptions, so a range or scenario view is needed

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits lets the learner build a benefit and total-cost-of-ownership comparison and see how ROI shifts when adoption or run costs change.

lessons.plain: Adoption and integration risk is the chance that a finished AI tool sits unused, gets worked around, or clashes with the way people already do their jobs. A model can score well and still fail if the people who must use it do not trust it, do not know how to use it, or were never told it was coming. Managing this risk means planning for the human side of the change: who is affected, how they will be prepared, how you will handle pushback, and how you will check that the new way of working is actually happening. It is planned alongside the technology, not added at the end.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dispatch team is told next month that they will get an AI tool suggesting which vehicle to send to each job. Name two things that could make the team ignore the tool even if its suggestions are accurate.
lessons.teach:
Change management is a structured way of moving people, processes, and roles from how work is done today to how it will be done with the new tool. User resistance is the set of reasons people push back: distrust of the output, fear of being blamed for errors, loss of control, extra workload, or not seeing any personal benefit. Adoption is the share of intended users who actually use the tool in their normal work. Integration risk is the risk that the tool does not fit with existing systems, handoffs, and approval steps. A training strategy is the plan for how each group learns: which roles need which skills, how they practise, and how refreshers happen after launch.
