Worked example: a claims team of 40 adjusters will use an AI tool that drafts settlement recommendations. Step 1: list the affected groups, which are adjusters, team leads, and auditors. Step 2: for each group, name the change. Adjusters must review and sign off, leads must update approval rules, and auditors need access to decision logs. Step 3: predict resistance. Adjusters fear being blamed for AI errors, so the plan keeps human sign-off and reports how often recommendations are overridden. Step 4: design training. Two hands-on sessions use past claims, and a three-adjuster pilot runs before full rollout. Step 5: set adoption measures, such as the weekly share of recommendations reviewed, and set a threshold that triggers extra coaching.

Common mistake: treating training as a single launch-day event, or assuming that accuracy alone will create adoption. Consequence: if people ignore the tool, the team keeps the manual process, the expected savings never arrive, and the ROI case built on usage fails. Worse, people may quietly work around the tool, so the logs no longer reflect the real decisions.

Adoption risk deserves the same planning rigour as technical risk, and its measures belong in the project's success criteria.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital's outpatient scheduling office plans an AI tool that suggests new appointments for slots freed by cancellations. Twelve front-desk schedulers will accept or edit each suggestion, four nurse managers set the daily overbooking limit, and six billing staff need each changed appointment to match the billing record. Step 1, listing the affected groups, is done: schedulers, nurse managers, and billing staff. Step 2, naming the change for each group, is done: schedulers must review suggestions, managers must update overbooking limits, and billing must confirm changed records. Step 3, predicting resistance, is done: schedulers fear being blamed when a patient is rebooked wrongly, so the plan keeps human confirmation and reports how often suggestions are edited. Step 4, designing training, is done: each scheduler completes two hands-on sessions using last quarter's cancellations, and a two-scheduler pilot runs before full rollout. Step 5, setting adoption measures and a trigger for extra coaching, is the one missing step and is left for you to complete.
choices: Track the weekly share of cancellation suggestions that schedulers review, and set a threshold below which nurse managers arrange extra coaching.
Remove the human confirmation step so schedulers are not blamed for errors, which raises adoption directly.
Run one launch-day training session, then review adoption again only after twelve months.
Report only the tool's suggestion accuracy each month, since accuracy is what drives adoption.
questions.why: Step 5 requires a measurable adoption measure with a threshold that triggers a specific response, and only the weekly review share with a coaching trigger does that.

questions.prompt: A dispatch company with 60 drivers rolls out an AI tool that proposes delivery routes. In change-management terms, which description best matches adoption?
choices: The percentage of routes the tool gets right when tested on last year's delivery data.
The number of hours the company spends on training sessions before the tool goes live.
The share of intended drivers who actually use the tool when planning their normal routes.
The gap between the tool's cost and the savings it is expected to produce in year one.
questions.why: Adoption is defined in the teaching text as the share of intended users who actually use the tool in their normal work, which is the driver-usage share described in option two.

questions.prompt: A warehouse with 90 pickers deploys an AI tool that suggests picking routes. Three months in, the dashboard shows high suggestion accuracy, but about a third of pickers still follow their paper routes, and the packing-station approval step has no link to the tool's output. What should the project manager examine first?
choices: Whether the tool should be retrained on a larger set of warehouse layouts before anyone else is asked to use it.
Whether the tool fits the existing handoff and approval steps, and how often routes actually followed match the tool's logs.
Whether the accuracy figure on the dashboard should be replaced with a cost figure for the paper routes.
Whether the pickers should be moved to a different shift so they stop using paper routes altogether.
questions.why: The symptoms point to integration risk, a mismatch between the tool and existing handoffs and approvals, and to logs that no longer reflect real decisions, so the first check is fit and actual usage.

questions.prompt: A bank with 45 loan officers rolls out an AI tool that drafts credit-decision notes. Training is one 90-minute session on launch day, with no hands-on practice and no refresher planned. Which outcome is the most likely consequence of this strategy?
choices: The bank's approval steps update themselves automatically once the tool is live.
Some officers quietly work around the tool, so the decision logs stop reflecting the real decisions made.
Officers adopt the tool faster because the session covers everything at once.
Officers' written notes become more accurate immediately, since the tool does the drafting.
questions.why: A single launch-day training event with no practice or refreshers is the common mistake named in the teaching text, and its typical consequence is quiet workarounds that make the logs unreliable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would plan for user resistance to a new AI tool before rollout, and name one limit or tradeoff of your plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every group whose work changes, not just the end users, and for each group I would write down what they will do differently. Then I would ask what would make them distrust or avoid the tool, such as fear of blame, extra steps, or unclear accountability. I would address those reasons directly: keep a human sign-off where accountability matters, share how often people override the tool and why, and run a small pilot with a few respected users before wider rollout. Training would be hands-on, based on real past cases, and followed by refreshers. I would track adoption, like the share of recommendations actually reviewed, and set a threshold that triggers coaching. The tradeoff is time and cost: pilots and sustained training slow the rollout and need budget, so I would agree with the sponsor how much delay is acceptable.
rubricPoints: Identifies all affected groups, not only the direct users
Names specific resistance reasons such as distrust, blame, or workload
Links training to real tasks and to ongoing refreshers rather than one launch event
Defines measurable adoption indicators tied to success criteria
States a concrete limit or tradeoff such as schedule, cost, or delayed benefits

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic rollout scenario with stakeholders adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers change management directly.

lessons.plain: Drafting an AI solution means sketching, before anyone builds anything, the rough shape of the system: which parts exist and how they connect (the high-level architecture), what information must flow into and out of the model and where it comes from (data flow requirements), and what kind of model or method is likely to fit the problem (the model or algorithmic approach). Think of it as a floor plan for a house. It is not the wiring diagram, but it shows the rooms, the doors, and the kind of foundation needed. The team and stakeholders are meant to question and revise the draft before money is committed to building it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A regional bus company wants an AI tool that predicts which buses will run late in the next hour so dispatchers can reassign drivers. Before reading anything more, what three things would you want written down in a first draft of the solution, and why would each one matter before anyone buys hardware?
lessons.teach: A high-level architecture is the main set of components in a proposed system and what each one is responsible for, such as data sources, storage, the step that turns raw records into model inputs (feature preparation), model training, the service that produces predictions, and the screen where people see them. Data flow requirements describe what data each component needs: its source, how fresh it must be, its format, its volume, who owns it, and what happens when it is missing. The model or algorithmic approach names the family of method (for example classification, regression, forecasting, or a simple rules baseline), why it suits the question, and how its output will be used. Drafting works because it forces decisions on paper, where they are cheap to check, instead of discovering them after a build. Worked example: the business question is whether each bus will be more than five minutes late in the next sixty minutes. Step one, the architecture: vehicle location feed, then ingestion, then stored history, then a feature builder (recent speed, schedule gaps, weather), then a weekly training job, then a prediction service running every minute, then the dispatcher screen. Step two, the data flow: location pings every thirty seconds, usable within two minutes of arrival; the timetable refreshed daily; at least twelve months of history; the fleet team as owner. Step three, the approach: a tree-based classifier on tabular features, compared against a simple baseline that assumes a late bus stays late, with output as a probability rather than a yes or no. Common mistake: naming a model first and treating the architecture as one box labelled AI, without the data flow or the decision the output drives. Consequence: if the prediction service needs fresher data than the feed delivers, dispatchers act on stale predictions and reassign the wrong drivers, so the draft must state that latency requirement explicitly.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility wants to flag pump stations likely to fail within 72 hours so maintenance crews can be scheduled. The draft architecture is: vibration sensors, then a telemetry gateway, then a stored history, then a feature builder (vibration trend, runtime hours, days since last service), then a monthly training job, then a scoring service running every 15 minutes, then the maintenance planner's dashboard. The data flow states that vibration readings arrive every 10 seconds and must be usable within 5 minutes, that service logs are updated weekly, that 24 months of history is kept, and that operations engineering owns the data. The step still missing is the model approach: what family of method is used, why it suits the question, and how its output is used. Which completion is correct?
choices: A tabular classifier giving a 72-hour failure probability, compared against a baseline that assumes the current state persists, with the probability ranking crews' inspection order
A convolutional image model applied to photographs of each pump, because images capture wear better than sensor numbers
An unsupervised clustering of pump readings into groups, reviewed by engineers afterwards, since no failure label needs to be predicted
A single fixed vibration threshold that flags pumps yes or no, which needs no comparison because a fixed rule is already simple
questions.why: The question asks for a per-pump probability over a stated window with a simple baseline to compare against, which a tabular classifier on the named features provides, while the other options either do not predict the stated outcome or skip the comparison.

questions.prompt: In a draft for a hospital forecasting when inpatients will be discharged, which architecture component is responsible for turning raw admission and lab records into the inputs the model reads?
choices: The feature preparation step, which builds model inputs from raw records
The ingestion queue that receives records from the hospital information system
The scoring service that returns predictions each hour
The discharge dashboard shown to bed managers
questions.why: Feature preparation is the component whose job is converting raw records into model inputs, while the other options handle display, prediction, or transport of data.

questions.prompt: A retailer drafts an AI system to flag returns that may be fraudulent. The draft lists the returns feed, storage, a model, and a flag service, but gives no freshness requirement for the returns feed, and the flag service is expected to run every 5 minutes. What is the most likely consequence if the feed actually arrives once a day?
choices: The model will train more slowly but its accuracy will be unchanged
The dashboard will show the flags in a different colour, which confuses staff
The storage costs will rise because the daily batch needs more disk space
The flags will be computed on refund records that are already processed, so the fraud team acts on stale flags
questions.why: A missing freshness requirement means the scoring service works from data that is too old to act on, so staff receive flags about returns that may already be settled; the other options describe effects unrelated to timeliness.

questions.prompt: A parcel company wants to forecast next-day parcel volume at each depot to plan staffing. Which model approach is best justified in the draft?
choices: A clustering of depots by size, used to assign the same staffing level to every depot in a cluster
A seasonal forecasting model that outputs a likely range, compared against a baseline that predicts the same weekday's volume from last week
A deep neural network that predicts an exact parcel count per depot with no baseline, since more complex models always perform better
A classifier that answers only whether volume will be above or below a fixed number, with no comparison
questions.why: Staffing needs a numeric forecast with uncertainty, and comparing against a simple same-weekday baseline shows whether the model adds value; the other options either lack a baseline, reduce the question to a coarse yes or no, or do not produce a forecast.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never drafted an AI solution what a high-level architecture, data flow requirements, and a model approach each cover, and name one limit or tradeoff of drafting these before the data has been checked.
lessons.modelAnswer: A high-level architecture is the set of main components and their jobs, showing how data moves from sources through storage and preparation to training and predictions, and finally to the people or systems that act on them. Data flow requirements state what each component needs: which source, how fresh, what format and volume, who owns it, and what happens when it is missing. The model approach names the method family, such as a classifier or forecaster, and why it fits, plus a simple baseline to compare against. The main limit is that the draft rests on assumptions about data we have not yet verified. If the feed is sparser or later than we assumed, the architecture and model choice may both change, so the draft should list those assumptions as things to test in a feasibility check before committing budget.
rubricPoints: Describes the high-level architecture as the main components and how data moves between them
Explains data flow requirements as source, freshness, format, volume, and ownership
Names a model or algorithmic approach and justifies it against the business question
Notes that the draft rests on unverified assumptions that need testing before committing resources

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a proposed initiative's architecture, data flow, and model choice in an exam-style situation adds the most, since no listed mission or engine covers drafting an AI solution.

lessons.plain: Before an AI project starts, the team has to agree on what good looks like and how the money side will judge it. Success criteria are the measures that show whether the project worked, such as how often the system gets things right or how many hours it saves. Key performance indicators, usually shortened to KPIs, are the few numbers you track to measure those criteria. A performance threshold is the line a number must cross to count as a pass, for example at least 90 percent accuracy on a test set. A business case is the written argument, checked with finance colleagues, that the benefits are worth the cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants an AI tool that flags late deliveries. Without looking anything up, what two or three numbers would you check six months later to decide whether the tool was worth keeping, and what level of each number would count as a clear success?
lessons.teach:
A success criterion is a statement of what must be true for the initiative to count as a win. A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measurable quantity you track to judge that statement, such as average days from order to delivery or the share of late deliveries caught before they happen. A performance threshold is the specific value a KPI must reach or stay within, such as catching at least 80 percent of late deliveries with no more than 5 percent false alarms. A business case is the written argument that expected benefits outweigh costs. Finance colleagues usually check its numbers because they own the budget and the rules for measuring returns.

Why it works: a threshold turns a vague hope into a decision rule. Without one, a team can declare victory whatever the result, and finance cannot compare the project with other spending. Good KPIs link to a business outcome such as money saved, hours recovered, or customers kept, rather than only to model metrics like accuracy, because a model can score well and still change nothing the business cares about.

Worked example: a dispatch team proposes a tool that predicts late deliveries. Step 1: the business outcome is fewer late deliveries that trigger refunds. Step 2: the KPI is the monthly count of refunds on late orders, with a current baseline of 400 per month. Step 3: the threshold is a drop to 300 or fewer within six months, and the model must catch at least 80 percent of late orders. Step 4: finance multiplies the avoided refunds by their cost and subtracts licence and staff costs to see whether the net benefit is positive.

Common mistake: choosing the threshold after seeing the results, or treating model accuracy as the only success measure. Consequence: if the threshold is set loosely, the project can be reported as successful while refunds stay flat, and the business case then fails at the first budget review.

questions.prompt: A call centre wants a tool that flags calls likely to become repeat calls. Its business case is partly worked. Step 1: the business outcome is fewer repeat calls, which cost overtime to handle. Step 2: the KPI (key performance indicator, a measurable quantity tracked to judge success) is the weekly count of repeat calls, with a current baseline of 220 per week. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: finance multiplies the avoided repeat calls by the cost per call and subtracts licence and staff costs to check that the net benefit is positive. Which option correctly completes the missing Step 3?
choices: Set the target after the pilot, at whatever level the pilot happens to reach, so it matches reality.
Customer satisfaction rises noticeably, as judged by service managers in a review after the first quarter of use.
The model's test-set accuracy reaches 92 percent, as reported by the data science team.
Repeat calls fall to 150 or fewer per week within four months, and the tool flags at least 75 percent of at-risk calls.
questions.why: Step 3 is the performance threshold, a specific value the KPI must reach plus the model's required catch rate, set in advance rather than from results or from a model metric alone.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team wants a tool to predict stockouts (items running out before the next restock). Which option is a performance threshold, as distinct from a KPI, a success criterion, or a model metric?
choices: Stockouts fall below 12 per month by March, and the model flags at least 85 percent of them in advance.
Stock availability matters to the business and should improve over time.
The model's precision score on last month's data.
The weekly stockout count, meaning the number of items that ran out of stock in a given week.
questions.why: A threshold is a specific value a KPI must reach or stay within, and this option gives exact numbers for both the outcome and the model's catch rate.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's fraud-review pilot is declared a success because the model's F1 score rose from 0.61 to 0.74, yet the monthly value of fraud losses did not change. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: The threshold should have been raised to an F1 of 0.90 so the team could show a larger improvement.
The team chose a model metric as the success measure and did not link the KPI to a business outcome such as losses avoided.
The F1 score was too low to start with, so the pilot needed a bigger dataset before any result could count.
The pilot was fine, and finance should accept model scores as proof of benefit because they are objective.
questions.why: Good KPIs link to business outcomes like money saved, because a model can score better and still change nothing the business cares about.

questions.prompt: A claims team at an insurer estimates its triage tool saves 1,200 staff hours a year, valued at $30 an hour, giving $36,000 of avoided cost. Licence costs are $20,000 a year and added staff costs are $15,000 a year. Using the finance method of subtracting costs from avoided costs, what is the annual net benefit?
choices: A net benefit of $71,000 a year, because the licence and staff costs are already sunk and should be ignored.
A net benefit of $1,000 a year, because avoided hours valued at $36,000 minus licence and staff costs of $35,000 leaves a positive result.
A net cost of $35,000 a year, because licence and staff costs are the only figures that finance counts.
A net benefit of $36,000 a year, since the hours saved are the whole return and costs are paid from a separate budget.
questions.why: Finance subtracts licence and staff costs from the avoided costs, so $36,000 minus $35,000 gives a positive net benefit of $1,000 a year.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says our AI project is a success because the model hit 95 percent accuracy. Explain to a teammate what is missing from that claim, and name one limit or tradeoff in setting thresholds before launch.
lessons.modelAnswer: Accuracy only tells us how often the model's predictions matched the test labels. It does not tell us whether the business changed. We need to know which KPI the project was meant to move, such as refunds on late orders or hours spent on manual checks, what its baseline was, and what threshold it had to reach, agreed before launch. A 95 percent score could still come from a test set that is easy or unrepresentative, and it could sit alongside flat refunds. The tradeoff when setting thresholds is that a demanding target may reject a project that would still pay back, while a lenient one lets weak results pass. Finance usually needs the threshold in money terms so the decision can be made against the cost of the work.
rubricPoints: Accuracy alone does not show a business outcome changed
A KPI needs a baseline and a threshold agreed before launch
Thresholds should be expressed in terms finance can use to compare costs and benefits
Setting thresholds involves a tradeoff between rejecting useful projects and approving weak ones

suggested.rationale: The core skill is articulating and defending success measures to a non-technical finance audience, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Before an AI project starts, someone has to ask what people, computers, and tools it will take, and whether the organization already has them. Skill requirements are the expertise the work needs, such as data engineering, model building, or privacy review. Infrastructure needs are the computing power, storage, and software environment the work runs on. A resource gap is the difference between what the project needs and what the team already has. When a gap is too large or too short-lived to fill by hiring, you bring in outside contractors. It is like planning a kitchen renovation: you list every trade, tool, and material, then decide which you can do yourself and which you will hire out.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of four engineers wants to build a model that reads customer emails and routes them to the right department. They have never handled personal data in a model and have no GPU server. Name two resource gaps you would check first, and say which one you would most likely hand to an outside contractor and why.
lessons.teach:
A resource plan answers three questions: what skills the work needs, what infrastructure it runs on, and where the team falls short. A skill requirement is a specific expertise a task needs, such as deploying a model to production. Infrastructure needs are the compute, storage, and tooling the work depends on, such as a training machine with a graphics processor (GPU) or a place to serve predictions to users. A gap is the difference between what is needed and what the team can supply. An outside contractor is an external specialist hired for a defined period or deliverable, usually when the skill is needed briefly, is hard to hire for, or is only needed once.

The reason to do this early is cost. A gap found in week two can be fixed with a phone call. The same gap found in month four can stop the project.

Worked example: a subscription company wants a churn-prediction model. Step 1: list the work by phase: data pipeline, feature building, model training, deployment, monitoring. Step 2: for each phase, name the skills. Step 3: compare with the team. A strong analyst knows SQL, but nobody has put a model into production, and nobody can do a privacy review. Step 4: list infrastructure. The data warehouse exists, training needs a GPU for about two weeks per quarter, and there is no model-serving environment. Step 5: decide each gap. Production deployment is needed once and is hard to hire for, so it goes to a three-month contractor with a knowledge-transfer clause. The privacy review is a short external engagement. The GPU is rented from the cloud rather than bought.

Common mistake: listing only the people who will build the model and forgetting data labeling, privacy and legal review, and the people who will run the system after launch. A model that nobody owns can be built and still never be used.

In a running system this shows up as a stalled launch: the model passes testing, but no one is on call for it, so it is never switched on.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics company wants a model that forecasts how many warehouse staff each site needs next week. Step 1: list the work by phase: data extraction, feature building, forecast training, scheduled retraining, and delivering forecasts to shift planners. Step 2: for each phase, name the skills needed, such as SQL for extraction, time-series validation for training, and job scheduling for retraining. Step 3: compare with the team. A strong SQL analyst and a Python developer who has built dashboards are on staff, but nobody has validated a time-series forecast or run scheduled retraining in production. Step 4: list infrastructure. The forecast model is small, so the nightly run fits on an existing CPU server, a GPU is not needed, and there is no scheduler set up for retraining. Step 5 is missing: decide how each gap is covered. Which decision is correct?
choices: Hire a contractor to own the forecast after launch, since ownership is a one-time setup task.
Hire a contractor for about six weeks to build and validate the forecast, with a knowledge-transfer clause, and name an internal owner for the ongoing scheduled run.
Leave the ownership gap until after launch, since the team can absorb it once the forecast is in use.
Buy a dedicated GPU server, since any forecasting job that runs on a schedule needs one.
questions.why: The time-series validation and scheduling gap is short and hard to hire for, so it goes to a contractor with knowledge transfer, while the ongoing run needs an internal owner because a contractor would leave.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital network wants a model that predicts which patients will miss follow-up appointments. Which item is an infrastructure need rather than a skill requirement?
choices: Ability to tune the decision threshold so the model flags the right number of patients
Experience running patient outreach calls after a flag is raised
A secure server with room for several years of scheduling records
Skill in writing a data-use policy that clinic staff can follow
questions.why: A secure server holding records is compute and storage the work depends on, whereas the other three describe expertise a person must have.

questions.prompt: A mid-size insurer needs a specialist in one rare model-monitoring tool for a single four-week setup, and never again after that. Which resource decision fits the criteria for using an outside contractor?
choices: Buy a larger server so that the team can compensate for not having the tool configured
Skip the monitoring setup and check the model by hand every month for as long as it runs
Hire a permanent staff member who will learn the tool and then maintain it indefinitely for the company
Contract the specialist for the four weeks and require a knowledge-transfer clause so staff can run it afterward
questions.why: A contractor is appropriate when the skill is needed briefly, is hard to hire for, or is needed only once, and a knowledge-transfer clause leaves the team able to run the tool later.

questions.prompt: A team lists its data scientists, data engineers, and a deployment specialist as the people needed for a new fraud model. It does not name anyone to be on call after launch. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The GPU bill falls because nobody is running the training jobs after launch
The model can pass testing and still never be switched on, because nobody owns its running
The privacy review is completed automatically by the cloud vendor at no extra cost
The model is retrained faster in the next cycle because the data engineers are already familiar with it
questions.why: Omitting the people who run the system after launch leaves a model that is built and tested but has no owner to switch it on and keep it running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether to hire a permanent employee, bring in an outside contractor, or reassign existing staff to fill a skills gap on an AI project. Name one limit or tradeoff of the contractor option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the skill the project needs and how long it is needed for. If the skill is needed for the whole project and will stay needed afterward, such as ongoing model monitoring, I would hire permanently or train an existing person. If the skill is needed for a short, defined piece, such as an initial deployment or a one-time privacy review, I would consider a contractor. I would reassign existing staff only if they already have most of the skill and the time to learn the rest. The main limit of a contractor is knowledge loss: when they leave, the know-how can leave with them. So I would require documentation and a handover plan in the contract, and make sure someone internal can run the system afterward.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes skills needed for the whole project from skills needed briefly or once
Compares hiring, contracting, and reassigning staff as separate options
Names a concrete limit of contractors, such as knowledge loss or dependence
Explains how to reduce that limit, such as handover or internal ownership

suggested.rationale: Choosing between hiring, contracting, and reassigning staff is a judgment the learner must articulate, and no listed mission or planned engine covers AI staffing decisions.

lessons.plain: Before an AI project builds anything, someone has to decide what data it needs: what kinds of information, in what shape, how much of it, and how clean it must be. Those choices come from the business goal. If the goal is to predict which delivery trucks will break down next month, you need sensor readings, maintenance records and truck details, enough history to cover several past breakdowns, and records accurate enough to trust. Writing this down early tells the team what to go looking for, and lets them tell leadership whether the data they have is good enough for the job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank wants an AI tool to flag loan applications that are likely to default. Before anyone collects data, what three or four things would you want written down about the data, and why would each one matter to the bank's goal?
lessons.teach:
A data requirement is a written statement of what data an AI solution needs before it is built. It covers four things. Data type is the kind of information, such as structured rows and columns, free text, images, or time-stamped sensor readings. Format is how the data is delivered, such as a database table, a CSV file, or JSON. Volume is how much data is needed, measured in records and in time span, and in particular how many examples exist of the outcome you want to predict. Quality standard is a measurable threshold, such as the maximum share of missing values, how fresh the data must be, or how closely it must match the source of truth.

The requirements are mapped to the business objective, meaning every item must trace back to a decision the business actually makes. Here is a worked example for the loan tool. Step one: the goal is to reduce losses from defaulted loans without rejecting good borrowers. Step two: the outcome to predict is whether a loan defaulted within twelve months, so the data must include a reliable default flag for each past loan. Step three: the type is structured, one row per loan, delivered as a table export. Step four: volume must include several thousand past loans and enough defaults, perhaps a few hundred, because a model cannot learn a rare outcome from forty examples. Step five: quality standards might require under two percent missing income values and a default flag that agrees with the payment ledger.

A common mistake is listing data by what is easiest to export rather than by what the decision needs. A running consequence follows: a model trained on data with a silently filled income gap can look accurate in testing and then misjudge applicants in production.

A requirement is only useful when every data item can be traced to a business decision and has a number that can be checked.

questions.prompt: A school district wants to flag students who are likely to fail a course so counselors can offer tutoring early. The goal is to give tutoring to students who need it without pulling in students who are doing fine. Step one: the outcome to predict is whether a student fails the course that term. Step two: the data must include a reliable pass or fail result for each student-course record. Step three: the data type is structured, one row per student per course per term, delivered as a CSV export from the gradebook. Step four is left for you to complete: the district records about 1,200 student-course records per year, and about 5 percent of those records end in failure. Which volume requirement completes step four?
choices: Only the failing course records, about 60 per year, since the model needs examples of the outcome alone.
One term of records, about 1,200 rows, which is enough because a pass or fail flag is simple to learn.
Ten years of records, about 12,000 rows, since more history always helps regardless of how many failures it contains.
Five years of records, about 6,000 rows, which yields roughly 300 failures to learn the outcome from.
questions.why: Volume covers both the number of records and the time span, and it must include enough examples of the outcome: five years gives about 6,000 rows, of which about 300 are failures, while one term or only the failures would leave too few examples or too little context.

questions.prompt: A hospital's data requirement for a readmission model states: the discharge date must match the electronic record audit log within 24 hours for at least 99 percent of records. Which of the four parts of a data requirement does this statement describe?
choices: Volume
Quality standard
Data type
Format
questions.why: It gives a measurable threshold (99 percent of records, within 24 hours) for how closely the data must match its source of truth, which is what a quality standard is.

questions.prompt: A retail team builds its data list for a product-return prediction model by exporting every table that its web analytics tool can produce easily, then sends the list to the project manager. What is the main flaw in this approach?
choices: The team should have requested images instead, since images always improve return prediction.
The format is wrong because CSV files cannot hold time-stamped records.
The list was built by what is easy to export rather than by the business decision the model supports, so items cannot be traced back to that decision.
The list has too few data types, because web analytics tools only produce free text.
questions.why: Every requirement item must trace to a decision the business makes, and listing data by ease of export breaks that link, which is the common mistake the unit warns about.

questions.prompt: A fleet company's delivery-time model has 9 percent of its delivery timestamps missing. The pipeline silently replaces each missing timestamp with the dispatch time, and the team reports good test accuracy. What is the best project-management response?
choices: Accept the result, because dispatch time is close enough to delivery time that the model cannot be misled.
Remove the missing rows and keep the fill, since the fill is harmless once rows are deleted.
Set a maximum missing-share standard, reject the silent fill, and check the model against live deliveries, since a silently filled gap can look accurate in testing and misjudge in production.
Ask for more years of data, since more history will automatically remove the effect of missing timestamps.
questions.why: A measurable missing-value threshold catches the gap, and the silent fill hides the problem during testing, so the risk appears only when the model makes live predictions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a business goal into a data requirement for an AI project, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would take.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the decision the business is trying to improve, then ask what outcome the model must predict and what information would plausibly inform that prediction. From there I write down the data type, delivery format, volume, and quality thresholds for each source. Volume needs particular care: I check how many examples exist of the rare outcome, not just the total row count. The main limit is that these requirements are set before the data is inspected, so some assumptions will be wrong. A field may be missing, or a threshold may be unrealistic for the source. So I treat the requirements as a first draft, check them against what the data actually contains, and report any gap to leadership in terms of what it means for the decision, such as fewer reliable predictions for a certain customer group.
rubricPoints: Links each data requirement back to a specific business decision or objective
Covers type, format, volume, and quality standards, not just the data source
Explains that volume should be judged by examples of the rare outcome
Names a limit such as assumptions made before the data is inspected
Describes checking requirements against real data and reporting gaps in business terms

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style data pipeline scenario to decide which requirements apply best fits this objective, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When an AI project needs data, someone has to answer three practical questions: who knows the data well enough to explain it, where the data actually lives, and whether those places are the right ones to draw from. Think of planning a big family dinner. You need someone who knows the recipes, a list of shops that sell the ingredients, and the old recipe book in the attic that still has useful notes. Data work is similar. Subject-matter experts are the people who understand what the numbers mean. Sources include internal systems the company runs, outside providers who sell or share data, and old archives kept from earlier systems. This objective is about finding and naming all three before anyone builds anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI team wants to predict late deliveries, and the only fresh data they know about sits in the dispatch system. Before anyone opens a file, what two other places or people would you ask about, and why?
lessons.teach:
Start with four definitions. A subject-matter expert (SME) is a person who understands what a dataset means in real operations: which fields are reliable, what a blank value stands for, and which system is the official record. An internal source is data your organization already produces and stores, such as transactional databases, logs, and reporting warehouses. An external provider is an outside party that supplies data, such as a price feed, a weather service, or a partner's records. A legacy archive is older data kept after the systems that produced it were replaced, often in old formats or backup files.

Why this matters: every data source has an owner and a meaning. A table name tells you little; the SME tells you the meaning, the date range, and the known gaps. Mapping each source to an SME before building lets the project avoid guessing.

Worked example: a team predicting equipment failures lists candidate sources. First, the maintenance database holds work orders; its SME is the maintenance supervisor, who confirms that a closed status means the machine was repaired. Second, sensor readings come from an internal historian; its SME is the controls engineer, who notes that sensors were recalibrated in 2021, so earlier readings are shifted. Third, a vendor offers failure statistics for similar machines; the team must check licence terms and whether the vendor's machines resemble theirs. Fourth, paper inspection records from 2008 to 2015 sit in an archive; they may record failures the database never captured, but they need digitising and an SME who can read the old forms.

Common mistake: treating the largest or most convenient source as the right one. Convenient data often lacks the history or meaning the model needs.

Consequence: if the team trains on the sensor data without knowing about the 2021 shift, the model learns a false pattern. Its predictions look accurate in testing but fail on live equipment. The source list is complete only when every entry has a named SME and a known meaning.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility wants to predict burst water mains. Its candidate sources are: (1) the customer billing system, whose SME is the billing team lead, who says a zero-consumption entry means the meter was not read and the bill was estimated; (2) pressure logs from district sensors, whose SME is the network engineer, who says the sensors switched from bar to kilopascal units in 2019; (3) a weather feed from a commercial provider, whose licence the legal team has confirmed allows model training; (4) handwritten repair logbooks from 1992 to 2003, stored in a basement archive. For sources 1 to 3 the team has already named an SME and recorded what each SME said about meaning. For source 4 the team has not yet done the one step that completes its entry: naming an SME. Which action completes the logbook entry?
choices: Scan all the logbooks and feed them straight into training, since they cover the most years
Name an SME who can read the 1992 to 2003 handwriting and explain the old crew codes, and record what that person says about gaps
Assume the crew codes match the billing system's codes because both describe field crews
Drop the logbooks because they are older than the current pressure sensors
questions.why: An archive entry is complete only when a named SME confirms what the old records mean, including their handwriting, codes, and known gaps.

questions.prompt: A colleague says an external provider is any data file the team downloads from the internet. Which correction is most accurate?
choices: An external provider is a data source only when the organization has paid a fee for it
External providers are always more accurate than internal sources because they serve many customers
An external provider is an outside party that supplies data to the organization, so the question is who supplies it, not how the file arrives
Any file downloaded from the internet counts as external, whatever its source, since it arrived from outside the building
questions.why: The teaching text defines an external provider by who supplies the data, an outside party, not by how the file is transferred or whether money changes hands.

questions.prompt: A retailer trains a demand model on a loyalty-program table. In 2017 the table was migrated from an older point-of-sale system, and the pre-2017 sales were left in a separate archive. The team uses only the migrated table because it is the newest and easiest to query. Which outcome is the main risk, and what step would have prevented it?
choices: The team has not asked the SME whether the 2017 migration changed how promotions were coded, so the model may learn a false trend that looks accurate in testing
The archive must be deleted because migrated data always replaces older data and duplicates it
The loyalty table must be discarded because any table migrated from another system is unusable for training
The model is fine because the migrated table is the official record by default, so no SME check is needed
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a source can look accurate in testing while carrying a meaning change, which only an SME can confirm before the model is built.

questions.prompt: A hospital is considering using a vendor's readmission statistics gathered in another state. Before deciding whether to use them, which step does the teaching text call for?
choices: Ask the billing team to rename the vendor's columns so they match the hospital's naming scheme
Check the licence terms and whether the vendor's patients and facilities resemble the hospital's
Use the statistics as they are, since vendors check their own figures before release
Replace the vendor's figures with the hospital's largest table so that all sources stay consistent
questions.why: For an external provider, the teaching text requires checking licence terms and whether the supplier's population resembles the project's population before use.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to the project how you would decide which data sources to use for an AI project, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on an external provider.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every place the answer to our question might live: internal systems, outside providers, and any legacy archives. For each one I would name the subject-matter expert who can tell us what the fields mean, how far back the history goes, and what changed over time. Then I would check whether the source covers the cases we care about, not just the common ones. The main limit of an external provider is that we do not control it. The feed can change format, stop without notice, or come with licence terms that restrict how we use it in a model. Before committing, I would confirm the contract allows our use and compare a sample against our internal records. Archives have the opposite issue: they may hold rare failures the live systems dropped, but they usually need cleaning and an expert who can interpret old formats.
rubricPoints: Names internal, external and legacy sources and says what each one is.
Pairs each source with a subject-matter expert who can explain its meaning.
States a concrete limit of external providers, such as licence terms or loss of control over the feed.
Notes that legacy archives may hold useful history but need cleaning or interpretation first.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic choice among internal, external and archive sources builds the judgement the exam tests better than reading a list.

lessons.plain: This is the setup of the workspace an AI team works in. It has three parts: compute, which is the processing power (processors, graphics chips, memory, and storage) needed to train or run a model; secure development environments, which are the controlled workspaces where people write code and handle data; and version control, which is a shared history of every change to code, configuration, and data-handling scripts. As a project manager you do not build these yourself. You make sure they exist, are sized for the work, are safe for sensitive data, and let anyone trace what changed, when, and by whom before the work starts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A data scientist says her model results cannot be reproduced because a colleague overwrote the code she ran last month. Which piece of infrastructure would have prevented this, and what would it have recorded?
lessons.teach:
Compute provisioning means requesting and configuring the processing capacity a project needs, such as processors, graphics chips (GPUs), memory, and storage, before work begins. A secure development environment is an isolated workspace with controlled access, approved software, and rules about where data may be copied. Version control is a system that records every change to code and scripts, along with the author, the time, and the reason, so that any earlier state can be restored and compared.

These matter together because an AI result is only trustworthy if someone can recreate it: the same code, the same settings, the same software versions, and the same data.

Worked example. A team must train a model on 40 GB of customer records. Step 1: estimate the work. Training on a laptop would take days, so the team requests one GPU machine with enough memory for the largest batch of data. Step 2: place that machine inside the approved network boundary, so the records never leave it, and grant access only to the named engineers, with read-only rights to the raw data. Step 3: store the cleaning scripts and settings in version control and tag the exact commit used for each model run. Step 4: record the software versions the environment uses.

Common mistake: the team gets a powerful machine, then copies the dataset onto personal laptops to make work easier, or shares one login among everyone. Both moves break the protected boundary and erase the record of who did what.

Consequence: when an auditor asks which data and code produced a deployed model, the team cannot answer, and the copied records sit outside the protected boundary, which is a privacy incident.

Sound workspace coordination keeps compute sized, access narrow, and every change traceable.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's team is building a delivery-delay model from 6 GB of shipment logs. Step 1: they estimated the work and requested one CPU server with 128 GB of memory, because the tabular data fits in memory and needs no graphics chips. Step 2: they placed the server inside the firm's approved network boundary, with read-only access to the logs for two named analysts. Step 3: they keep the feature-building scripts in version control. Step 4: they recorded the software library versions in the environment. One step is still missing before anyone can later explain a deployed model's result. Which step is it?
choices: Buy a second GPU server so that training finishes sooner
Replace the two named analyst accounts with one shared login
Export a copy of the logs to a shared drive for the business team
Tag the exact version-control commit used for each model run
questions.why: Tagging the exact commit for each run ties a specific model result to the exact code that produced it, which is what makes the result recreatable and auditable.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines version control as used in an AI workspace?
choices: A system that records each change to code and scripts with its author, time, and reason, so earlier states can be restored and compared
A log that tracks how much processor time each training job consumed
A nightly copy of the full dataset stored on a separate disk
A scheduler that automatically assigns the fastest available graphics chip to each job
questions.why: Version control is defined by recording every change with author, time, and reason so that any earlier state can be restored and compared, and only the third option describes that.

questions.prompt: A data scientist in a secure workspace, where data cannot be copied out, exports a 2 GB sample of customer records to a personal laptop because experiments run faster there. What is the most accurate consequence?
choices: The sample now sits outside the protected boundary, which is a privacy incident even if the code remains traceable
Nothing changes, because a 2 GB sample is too small to matter
The model must be discarded and retrained from scratch
The version control history is erased and cannot be recovered
questions.why: Copying records outside the approved boundary breaks the protection rules and creates a privacy incident regardless of the sample's size, while the code history itself is unaffected.

questions.prompt: A team has an 800 MB spreadsheet of past sales records and a simple regression that finishes in seconds on a standard laptop. Which compute decision best follows the idea of provisioning sized to the work?
choices: Request the largest GPU cluster available, so that no future growth causes a shortage
Estimate the work, then use a modest machine inside the approved boundary, since no graphics chip is needed for this job
Copy the spreadsheet onto several personal laptops so that each engineer can run experiments
Skip estimating the work, because simple jobs never need planning
questions.why: Provisioning should match the estimated work, so a modest machine kept inside the approved boundary fits this job, while the other options either oversize compute or break the access rules.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a project manager should care about where the model training environment runs and who can access it before the team starts building, and name one limit or tradeoff of locking the environment down.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before building starts, the environment decides three things: whether the team has enough processing power to finish on time, whether sensitive data stays inside the approved boundary, and whether results can be reproduced later. If the training environment sits outside the approved network or is open to too many people, we may copy sensitive records into places we cannot control, and that becomes a compliance problem during the project. Locking the environment down has a real tradeoff, though: tight access slows engineers who need to experiment, and every request for a new library or extra compute goes through an approval step. As the project manager, I plan for that approval time in the schedule and agree in advance which requests can be self-service and which need review, so the controls protect the data without stalling the work.
rubricPoints: Explains that the environment determines compute capacity, data boundary, and reproducibility.
Names a concrete risk of an unprotected environment, such as copies of sensitive data leaving the boundary.
States a real tradeoff of tight access, such as slower experimentation or approval delays.
Describes a practical coordination step, such as planning approval time or setting self-service rules.

suggested.rationale: Coordinating infrastructure is best shown by explaining the access and reproducibility tradeoffs in your own words, and no listed mission covers AI workspace setup.

lessons.plain: Before an AI project trains or tests anything, someone has to gather the data it needs and confirm the team is allowed to use that data in the planned way. Think of it like a kitchen: before cooking, you check that the ingredients are yours to use, that they have not expired, and that no guest has an allergy you must respect. For data, the checks cover three things: whether the terms of the source allow this use (usage licensing), whether personal information is handled the way privacy and data protection laws require, and whether the people doing the work actually have permission to reach the data. Skipping these checks can stop a project late, or force a rebuild after the data has already been used.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has a large, clean set of customer emails they want to use to train a model. What would you check before the first line of training code runs, and why?
lessons.teach:
Usage licensing is the set of terms, usually in a contract or data agreement, that says what you may do with a dataset: train a model, share it, use it commercially, or keep it after a project ends. Personal data is any information that identifies a person or can reasonably be linked to one, such as names, email addresses, or account numbers. Data protection regulations are laws that set rules for collecting, storing, and using personal data; the GDPR in Europe is one example. Purpose limitation is the principle that data collected for one reason should not be reused for an unrelated reason without a legal basis. Access rights define who may read, copy, or change the data, normally granted by role and recorded so it can be audited.

These checks work as gates. Data that fails a gate cannot be used, however accurate or complete it is.

Worked example: a team wants to train a churn model on last year's support transcripts. Step 1, licensing: the transcripts were produced under a support contract that permits internal service improvement but not sale to third parties, so internal model training may fit, but the contract owner must confirm it. Step 2, privacy: the transcripts contain names, emails, and account numbers, so they are personal data; the team must remove or mask identifiers and confirm that the original support purpose covers model training. Step 3, access: only the named analysts in the approved group get read access, inside a restricted project area rather than on personal laptops. Step 4, record: the source, the permitted purpose, the masking applied, and the approver are written down.

Common mistake: treating 'we already hold this data' as permission to use it for any purpose. The consequence is that the model gets built, the legal review then blocks deployment, and the team must retrain on compliant data, sometimes deleting derived artifacts along the way.

No data is ready for modelling until its licence, privacy status, and access rights have been checked and recorded.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain collected loyalty-card purchase records so it could issue reward points. A data team now wants those records to train a demand-forecasting model. The team has already confirmed that the loyalty terms allow internal use, replaced card numbers with masked tokens, limited read access to a named analytics group inside a restricted project area, and written down the source, masking applied, and approver. The one gate not yet done is checking whether the reason the data was collected, issuing rewards, covers forecasting. What is the outstanding step?
choices: Confirming under purpose limitation that the reward-collection reason covers forecasting, or obtaining a legal basis if it does not
Copying the records to a second storage location so the forecasting team has a backup
Nothing remains; all gates are complete once the record is written
Checking that the purchase totals are accurate by sampling a few hundred rows
questions.why: Purpose limitation requires confirming that a new use such as forecasting is compatible with the original collection purpose or has a legal basis, and the other choices are either already done or unrelated to the gates.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines usage licensing for a dataset?
choices: A law that sets rules for how personal data may be collected and stored
The contract or data agreement terms that state what you may do with the dataset, such as training a model, sharing it, or keeping it after a project ends
A principle that data collected for one reason must not be reused for an unrelated reason
The recorded list of which people may read, copy, or change the dataset
questions.why: Usage licensing is defined in the teaching text as the set of terms in a contract or agreement that says what you may do with a dataset.

questions.prompt: A transit authority holds two years of fare-card tap records. The names were deleted, but each record still contains the card's account number. An analyst says no privacy check is needed because no names remain. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: No privacy check is needed, since removing names makes the records anonymous
Privacy only matters for data shared outside the organisation, so the check can be skipped for internal use
The records remain personal data, because an account number can be linked to a person, so the privacy check still applies
Only the access rights need checking, because accuracy is the only gate that applies to fare records
questions.why: The teaching text defines personal data as anything that identifies a person or can reasonably be linked to one, and lists account numbers as an example, so the records still need the privacy gate.

questions.prompt: A small startup receives a dataset from a vendor under an agreement that permits evaluation only. The team now wants to train its production model on it. What should it do first?
choices: Keep the data and begin training while the contract is reviewed later
Treat the data as cleared because the vendor chose to send it
Stop before training, check whether the agreement permits training use, and get permission from the vendor if it does not
Train the model now, since the team already holds the file and the data is accurate
questions.why: Usage licensing governs what you may do with the data, and an evaluation-only agreement does not by default permit training, so the licence must be checked and any needed permission obtained before modelling.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a dataset can be high quality and still be unusable for an AI project. Name one limit or tradeoff the team must weigh when resolving this.
lessons.modelAnswer: A dataset can be accurate, complete, and well labelled and still be unusable because the team may not have the right to use it for this purpose. The licence might allow internal reporting but not model training, or the data might contain personal information collected for a different reason. Quality checks answer whether the data is good; compliance checks answer whether we may use it at all, and both must pass. The main tradeoff is speed against safety: removing or masking identifiers and getting approval takes time and can reduce the data's usefulness, sometimes sharply. The right move is to record the permitted purpose, apply the needed masking, and get the owner's sign-off before training, rather than discovering the problem after a model has been built and deployed.
rubricPoints: Separates data quality (accuracy, completeness) from legal permission to use the data.
Names usage licensing or purpose limitation as a specific gate the data must pass.
Identifies personal data and the need for masking, access control, or approval.
States a real tradeoff, such as time or reduced usefulness against compliance risk.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style data pipeline scenario, with licensing, privacy, and access decisions to make, adds the most to this objective beyond reading the rules.

lessons.plain: Before an AI model learns anything, someone has to check the data it will learn from. Overseeing data evaluation means judging that data on a few plain tests: is it correct, is it complete, does it agree with itself, and does it cover the people or situations the model will serve? It also means looking at the data's shape and summary numbers first, a step called exploratory data analysis, so surprises show up before they become model mistakes. Think of a building inspector walking the site before the builders pour concrete. Problems found now are cheap; problems found after launch are expensive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A hospital wants an AI tool to flag patients at risk of readmission. Its training records have no missing values at all in the file. Does that mean the data is ready to use? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Data quality is judged on dimensions, which are separate ways data can be wrong. Accuracy means each value matches what is true in the real world. Completeness means the required values and records are present. Consistency means the same fact agrees everywhere it appears, across tables, sources, units, and time. A dataset can score well on one dimension and badly on another, so each needs its own check.

Bias and gap analysis asks whether the data represents the population the model will actually serve. Compare the share of each group in the training data with its share in the real customer base. A group that is badly underrepresented is a gap, and a model trained on it will often perform worse for that group, even when its overall score looks good.

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) means summarizing the data before modeling: counts of missing values, distributions, outliers, and comparisons between slices. It finds problems that the quality rules miss.

Worked example. A telecom churn dataset has 50,000 accounts. Step one, completeness: monthly_charges is blank for 4 percent of rows, so 2,000 rows. Step two, consistency: tenure_months disagrees with contract_start_date in 900 rows. Step three, accuracy: a spot check of 100 sampled rows against the billing system finds 7 wrong, an estimated 7 percent error rate that needs investigating. Step four, gap: rural accounts are 3 percent of training rows but 20 percent of live customers. Step five, EDA: a histogram shows 1,200 rows with monthly_charges of exactly zero, which may be real free plans or a loading error.

Common mistake: dropping the blank rows without checking which rows they are. If the blanks cluster in rural accounts, the cleaned file quietly removes the group the model most needs to learn.

Consequence: the model reports strong overall accuracy, rural customers get poor predictions in production, and the average hides the problem. The data is not ready until each dimension, gap, and odd pattern has been checked and either fixed or documented.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company has 80,000 delivery records used to predict late arrivals. Step one, completeness: courier_rating is blank for 2,400 records, which is 3 percent. Step two, consistency: the restaurant_zone code differs between the orders table and the dispatch table in 610 records. Step three, accuracy: a spot check of 120 sampled orders against the restaurants' own tickets finds 11 wrong. Your task is to state the estimated error rate from step three and what it means for the next action. Step four, EDA: a histogram of prep_minutes shows 300 orders at exactly zero minutes.
choices: About 9 percent, so the 11 wrong rows can be dropped and the rest trusted
About 1 percent, so accuracy is fine and no investigation is needed
About 11 percent, which is the count of wrong rows and must be fixed before modeling
About 9 percent, which needs investigating before the data is used
questions.why: 11 wrong out of 120 sampled is about 9.2 percent, and the teaching text treats a rate like this as a signal to investigate rather than something to ignore or simply drop.

questions.prompt: In a hospital dataset, the same clinic visit is dated 3 March in the scheduling table and 5 March in the billing table. Which data quality dimension is violated?
choices: Completeness, because a required value is missing
Accuracy, because the value fails to match the real world
Bias, because one group is underrepresented
Consistency, because the same fact disagrees across tables
questions.why: Consistency means the same fact agrees everywhere it appears, and here one visit date differs between two tables, while the scenario gives no missing values or group shares.

questions.prompt: A bank trains a loan model on 12,000 past applications. Only 6 percent of them come from small-business owners, but 22 percent of applications arriving live are from that group. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The data is complete and consistent, so the mismatch between training and live shares does not matter for the model
A gap: small-business applicants are 6 percent of training rows but 22 percent of live applications, so the model may perform worse for them even when its overall score looks good
Dropping the small-business rows from the live data would be the simplest way to make the training and live shares agree
The model's overall accuracy of 91 percent shows it serves small-business applicants well, so no action is needed before deployment
questions.why: A group that is badly underrepresented in training is a gap, and the teaching text warns that such a model often performs worse for that group even when the overall score looks good.

questions.prompt: A team cleans a sensor dataset of 40,000 readings by dropping every row with a blank value. The blanks make up 5 percent of rows, and all of them come from one factory. What is the main risk, and what should the team do first?
choices: The blanks signal accuracy errors, so the cleaned file is more accurate and the team can skip any further checks
Nothing is at risk, because removing 5 percent of rows is always safe when the rest of the data looks clean
Check which rows are blank before dropping them, because the cleaned file may quietly remove the factory the model most needs to learn
Exploratory analysis is unnecessary here, because the factory cluster can only be detected by a bias check after modeling
questions.why: The teaching text's common mistake is dropping blank rows without checking which rows they are, because a cluster of blanks in one group removes that group from the training data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a dataset with no missing values can still be unfit for training an AI model. Name one dimension beyond completeness and one limit of checking only a sample.
lessons.modelAnswer: A file with no blanks only shows completeness. Data can be complete and still wrong: a value can be filled with a default, a placeholder, or a stale number, which is an accuracy problem. Consistency is a separate check: the same customer's start date may disagree between the billing and contract tables, and a model will learn from both versions. Beyond quality, the file may simply not represent the people the model will serve, which is a gap. I would also flag the limit of sampling: spot-checking 100 rows gives an estimate of the error rate, not a guarantee, and errors clustered in one segment can hide inside a small sample. So before we call it ready, we check accuracy on a sample, consistency across tables, and coverage by group, and we write down what we found.
rubricPoints: Completeness only checks whether values are present, not whether they are correct.
Accuracy and consistency need their own checks, against a trusted source or across tables.
Coverage gaps appear when group shares in the training data differ from the live population.
A sample gives an estimate and can miss errors concentrated in small segments.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a messy data pipeline scenario builds the judgment this objective needs, and no listed mission covers AI data quality directly.

lessons.plain: Before an AI project builds anything, someone has to ask a plain question: do we already have the data we need, and is it good enough for the job? Checking this is like checking ingredients before promising a dinner party. You compare what the project needs (the right information, enough of it, accurate and recent) with what actually exists, and you note the gaps. The second half of the skill is reporting the answer to leaders in terms of cost, timing, and risk rather than technical detail. A clear 'not yet, and here is what it would take' is more useful than a vague 'probably fine'.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants a model that predicts which customers will cancel next month, and the only history they have comes from a billing system that was changed two years ago. Before anyone trains anything, what is the first concern you would raise about whether that data is ready, and why?
lessons.teach:
Data readiness means whether the data you can actually get is fit for a specific purpose. A dataset can be large and still not be ready. Readiness is judged against the solution's needs, which come from the business question: what decision will the AI support, and what information does that decision require?

Three terms matter here. Coverage is whether the data includes the cases and time periods the solution will face. Quality is whether the values are correct, complete, and consistent with each other. Access is whether the team is allowed to use the data, in the form and timeliness the solution needs, under the rules that apply to it.

Why does this work as a check? Each gap maps to a specific cost. Missing history means the model cannot learn a pattern. Inconsistent definitions mean two teams count the same thing differently. Restricted access means the project stalls later, after money is spent.

Worked example: a team wants to predict late deliveries. Step 1: the business need is a warning 24 hours ahead. Step 2: the required fields are order time, route, and carrier. Step 3: the data has those fields, but carrier names changed in March, and timestamps are recorded in local time for only one region. Step 4: the verdict is 'partially ready'. The fix is to standardise carrier names and time zones, which is a defined, costed task.

The common mistake is reporting 'we have lots of data' as if that were readiness. Volume is not fit for purpose.

The consequence shows up in a running system. If a model trains on the unfixed data, it can look accurate in testing while failing in production, because live data no longer matches what it learned from.

Leaders need the same facts in business terms: what is ready, what is not, what it costs to close each gap, and what risk remains if the project proceeds anyway.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic group wants an AI tool that flags appointments likely to be missed (no-shows) at least 48 hours ahead, so staff can overbook safely. The solution needs booking date, reminder status, and each patient's past no-show count. The group has three years of records from two clinics. Step 1: the business need is a flag 48 hours ahead so staff can decide on overbooking. Step 2: the required fields are booking date, reminder status, and past no-show count. Step 3: both clinics have all three fields, but Clinic A records a missed visit as 'no-show', while Clinic B records it as 'cancelled' with no separate flag, so the two clinics count the same event differently. Step 4 is missing. Which conclusion completes the assessment?
choices: Partially ready: the fix is to map Clinic B's 'cancelled' records to the same no-show definition used by Clinic A, a defined and costed task.
Not ready: the group must collect five new years of data before any work starts.
Ready: three years of records is plenty, so the labels will sort themselves out during training.
Ready: both clinics store every required field, so access and definitions are not a concern.
questions.why: Inconsistent definitions are a quality gap that can be closed with a specific, costed standardisation task, so the honest verdict is partially ready with that fix named.

questions.prompt: In the context of data readiness, what does 'coverage' mean?
choices: Whether the values in the data are correct, complete, and consistent with each other.
Whether the team is legally and contractually allowed to use the data in the required form.
How many rows and columns the dataset contains compared with the storage budget.
Whether the data includes the cases and time periods the solution will face in use.
questions.why: The teaching text defines coverage as whether the data includes the cases and time periods the solution will face, which is distinct from quality and access.

questions.prompt: A retail chain has 2 million sales rows from its 80 existing stores, but no rows from the 12 stores opened in 2023. The solution must forecast demand for any store, including new ones. Which assessment best fits this situation?
choices: Quality problem: the values need cleaning, so run a consistency check on the sales amounts.
Coverage gap: the data does not include the kind of cases the solution will face, so the forecast for new stores is unsupported until that is addressed.
Volume is sufficient: two million rows is far more than the model needs, so the data is ready.
Access problem: the team needs permission to pull sales data from the chain's point-of-sale system.
questions.why: The missing stores mean the data does not cover the cases the solution must handle, which is a coverage gap, and large volume does not fix it.

questions.prompt: A team trains a demand model on data recorded before a unit-of-measure change, where quantities switched from cases to single units partway through the history. In testing the model looks accurate, but in production its predictions are badly off. What is the most likely cause, based on the consequence described for running systems?
choices: The business question changed after training, so the model answers the wrong decision.
The model was tested on too few rows to show the true error rate.
The live data no longer matches what the model learned from, so the test accuracy did not carry over to production.
Access to the production database was restricted, which slowed the predictions down.
questions.why: When a model trains on data that does not match what it will see live, testing can look accurate while production fails, because the live data differs from the training data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked on an AI project how you would decide whether the available data is ready for a solution, and how you would tell a non-technical sponsor the answer. Name at least one limit or tradeoff in your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the decision the solution supports, then list the fields and history that decision needs, and compare that list with what we actually hold. For each gap I would say whether it concerns coverage, quality, or access, because each has a different fix. To the sponsor I would avoid technical terms and give three things: whether the data is ready for this purpose, what it would take to make it ready in time and within budget, and what goes wrong if we start early. The tradeoff is that a quick check is not a full assessment.
