Some quality problems only appear when the data is profiled in depth, so I would present the readiness verdict as a current judgement with a stated confidence level rather than a guarantee.
rubricPoints: Readiness is judged against the specific business decision and the data that decision requires, not against data volume alone.
Gaps are sorted into coverage, quality, or access, since each has a different remedy.
Leadership is told what is ready, what it costs to close gaps, and the remaining risk, in business terms.
The verdict is stated with its limits, since a quick check can miss quality problems found only through deeper profiling.

suggested.rationale: Conveying a data readiness verdict to leadership in business terms is a spoken explanation skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: When you start an AI project, one early choice is the kind of learning approach to use. Some methods learn from examples where the right answer is already recorded. Others look for patterns in data with no answers attached, or learn by trying actions and seeing which ones earn rewards. Each kind brings different tradeoffs: how much data and effort it needs, how hard it is to build and run, and how easily people can understand why it made a given output. You do not pick the algorithm yourself, but you need to know which tradeoff the team is accepting and whether it fits the business need, the risk, and the people who must trust the result.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank wants a tool that flags likely fraudulent card payments, and it has five years of past payments already marked as fraud or not fraud. Before any teaching, which broad learning approach would you expect the team to try first, and what concern would you raise about the most powerful version of that approach?
lessons.teach:
Supervised learning means the model learns from examples where the correct answer is already recorded, called labels. You show it many past cases with their outcomes, and it learns a mapping from inputs to outcomes that it applies to new cases. Unsupervised learning works on data with no labels. The method looks for groups or unusual patterns, such as clustering customers by buying behaviour, and a person decides what those groups mean. Reinforcement learning is different: an agent takes actions in an environment, receives a reward or penalty for each, and gradually learns a strategy that earns more reward over time.

Interpretability means how easily a person can see why a model produced a particular output. Complexity means how many internal parts the model has and how much data, compute and tuning it needs. These often pull against each other. A shallow decision tree or a linear model can be read by a human, while a large neural network may be more accurate on messy data but is hard to explain.

Worked example: the bank has five years of payments labelled fraud or not fraud. Step 1: labels exist, so supervised learning fits. Step 2: the team trains a shallow decision tree first, which yields rules a fraud analyst can read. Step 3: they compare it with a deep network that scores slightly higher on the held-out test set. Step 4: they weigh that small accuracy gain against the need to explain declined payments to customers and regulators, and they record the choice and its reason.

Common mistake: choosing the most powerful model by default because it scores best on one metric, without asking whether anyone can justify its decisions or maintain it.

In a running system, an opaque model that is hard to debug may keep flagging legitimate customers after a shift in spending patterns, and the team may not learn why for weeks. Choosing the technique is a decision about how the system will be explained, checked and corrected after it goes live.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank has donor records (gift size, how often each donor gives, preferred pickup day) with no outcome labels attached, and it wants to find donor types to plan outreach. Step 1: no labels exist, so supervised learning does not fit and unsupervised learning does. Step 2: the team runs the method and it returns five groups of donors. Step 2 is the step that says what to do with those five groups, and it is left blank here. Which action completes step 2?
choices: Treat the five groups as labels and train a deep network to predict them for new donors
Discard the groups, because data without labels cannot be used to draw any conclusion
Add a reward for each donor retained so the groups improve over time through trial and error
Have a staff member review each group's typical donors and decide what the group represents
questions.why: Unsupervised methods only find groups or unusual patterns, and a person decides what those groups mean, so reviewing and naming each group completes the step.

questions.prompt: A customer support team has 40,000 past call transcripts, and each one has a recorded field showing whether the issue was resolved on the first call. The team wants a model that predicts resolution for new calls. Which technique fits best, and why?
choices: Supervised learning, because each past case already has a recorded outcome that the model can learn from
Supervised learning, but only if the team also removes the outcome field before training
Unsupervised clustering, because transcripts are text and have no structure to learn from
Reinforcement learning, because the model should earn reward for each resolved call
questions.why: The recorded resolution field is a label, and labelled past cases are what supervised learning needs; the other options either misread the data or wrongly remove the labels.

questions.prompt: A lender builds a loan-approval model that scores highest on the validation set, but it is a very large model with thousands of interacting parts. Applicants have a legal right to a reason for a refusal, and the team has no plan for explaining individual decisions. What is the most significant risk of this choice?
choices: The model will fail only if reinforcement rewards are set incorrectly
The model cannot be used at all because any model with a validation score is unlawful
The model will train too quickly and overfit the applicants' data
The team may be unable to explain or correct individual refusals, even though the score was high
questions.why: Choosing the top-scoring but opaque model without asking whether decisions can be explained and maintained is the common mistake, and it leaves the team unable to justify or fix refusals.

questions.prompt: A delivery company is building a system that picks the dispatch order for its vans. Each time a van completes a route on time, the system gets a positive score, and each late delivery or missed window gives a negative score. Over many simulated days the system gradually learns a dispatch strategy that earns more score overall. Which learning type best describes this system?
choices: Unsupervised learning, because the system groups vans by similar routes
Supervised learning, because the company has recorded past dispatch outcomes
Reinforcement learning, because the system stores each route as a labelled example
Reinforcement learning, because an agent acts in an environment and learns from rewards and penalties
questions.why: Learning from rewards and penalties over repeated actions is reinforcement learning; the recorded outcomes here are not used as labels for a supervised mapping, and the system is not clustering.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we are not simply using the most accurate model for our loan-review tool. Explain to them, in your own words, how supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning differ, and name the main limit or tradeoff we would accept by choosing a more interpretable model.
lessons.modelAnswer: Supervised learning uses past examples that already have the right answer attached, so the model learns to predict those answers for new cases. Unsupervised learning has no answers attached and looks for structure, such as groups, which people then interpret. Reinforcement learning learns by acting and receiving rewards or penalties over time. For the loan tool we have labelled past decisions, so supervised learning is the natural fit. The most accurate model is often the hardest to explain. If we choose a simpler, interpretable model, we accept that it may score a little lower on accuracy. In return we can give applicants and regulators a clear reason for each decision, and we can find and fix problems faster when the model misbehaves. We should document that tradeoff and test whether the accuracy gap actually matters for the business.
rubricPoints: Supervised learning uses labelled past examples to predict known outcomes
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data and needs people to interpret it
Reinforcement learning learns from rewards or penalties through trial and action over time
A more interpretable model may give up some accuracy in exchange for explainability and easier debugging

suggested.rationale: Explaining the learning approach and its tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective.

lessons.plain: Model QA/QC means checking that an AI model is good enough and trustworthy before people rely on it. QA (quality assurance) is the set of planned rules that prevent problems, such as agreeing in advance how a model will be tested. QC (quality control) is the testing itself, which checks the model's actual results against those rules. Configuration management keeps a written record of exactly which data, settings and code produced each model, so results can be repeated later. Peer review means other people read the model design and challenge it before it moves forward. A project manager does not run every test personally, but makes sure the testing rules exist, are followed, and are documented.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team reports that their new model scores 94 percent on the test data. Before anyone celebrates, what three things would you want to know about how that score was produced?
lessons.teach:
A test protocol is a written plan that states what will be tested, on which data, what result counts as a pass, and who signs off. A holdout test set is data kept aside and never used to build or tune the model, so it can act as a fair exam. Configuration management is the habit of recording the exact code version, the data snapshot, the feature list, the settings and the random seed (the starting number that makes random steps repeatable) for every model run. Peer review is an independent check of the design by someone who did not build it.

This works because a score means little unless someone else can reproduce it and the model never saw the answers during building. Worked example: a customer churn model reports 94 percent accuracy. Step 1: the protocol says the holdout set was frozen before training; the record confirms it. Step 2: the configuration record shows data snapshot version 3, seed 42 and a feature list. Step 3: the reviewer notices a feature called cancelled_on, which is only filled in after a customer has already left, so the model is cheating by looking at the future. This is called leakage. The team removes the feature, reruns under the same protocol, and accuracy falls to 71 percent. The call is no-go until the leaking feature is removed and the rerun is documented.

A common mistake is re-tuning the model again and again against the holdout set until the score looks good. Once the test set has been used to make choices, it is no longer an independent test, and the reported number is inflated. The consequence in a running system is that the model looks strong in review, then performs far worse on real customers, and nobody notices until revenue or trust is lost.

A model result is trustworthy only when its protocol was fixed in advance, its configuration can be reproduced, and an independent reviewer has checked the design for leakage and unsafe shortcuts.

questions.prompt: A credit union builds a loan default model. Its written test protocol, saved before training, says the holdout set is 8,000 loans from late 2023, frozen and never used for building or tuning. Step 1: the record confirms the holdout was frozen before training. Step 2: the configuration record shows code tag v2.4.1, data snapshot 6, seed 2024 and a 38-feature list. Step 3: the reviewer finds a feature called collections_flag_date, which is only filled in after a loan has already entered collections, so the model is looking at the future and is leaking the answer. Step 4 is missing. The team's reported accuracy is 91 percent before the fix. What is the correct Step 4?
choices: Keep the 91 percent figure, since the holdout was frozen before training, and ship the model.
Replace the holdout with a fresh random split from the same 2023 loans so the score rises before the review.
Retune the decision threshold on the holdout until accuracy returns to 91 percent, then ship the model.
Remove collections_flag_date, rerun on the same frozen holdout under the same protocol, and document the new result before any go decision.
questions.why: The leaking feature must be removed and the model rerun under the unchanged protocol on the same frozen holdout, with the honest new result documented before a go call is made.

questions.prompt: A product team describes its holdout test set in a status update. Which description matches the idea in the teaching text?
choices: Data kept aside and never used to build or tune the model, so it works as a fair test.
A copy of the training data with the labels hidden from the builders.
Any dataset the independent reviewer has not yet read through.
The most recent rows used for early stopping during training.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a holdout set as data kept aside that is never used to build or tune the model, which is what makes it a fair exam.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain's demand forecast model has a configuration record listing the code commit, the data snapshot and the feature list, but no random seed. A second team reruns it and gets a different score. Which gap most directly explains the mismatch?
choices: The model used too many trees, so results vary by run.
The seed was not recorded, so random steps cannot be repeated exactly.
The reviewer did not sign the test protocol before the rerun.
The holdout set was too small to produce a stable score.
questions.why: A seed is the starting number that makes random steps repeatable, and without it the run cannot be reproduced to the same result.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud model reaches 96 percent on its holdout set after the team repeatedly adjusts settings while checking that same holdout score. What is the most accurate assessment of that number?
choices: It is a reliable figure because the team checked the score many times.
It is inflated, because the holdout has been used to make choices and is no longer independent.
It is accurate, provided the reviewer signed off on the final settings.
It is only a concern if the holdout set was later used as training data.
questions.why: Once the holdout has been used to choose settings it stops being an independent test, so the reported 96 percent overstates how the model will perform on live traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a model's reported evaluation result is trustworthy enough to move forward, and name one limit of the check you are using.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not look at the headline score first. I would ask whether the test protocol was written and agreed before training, and whether the holdout data was truly kept away from the model during building and tuning. Then I would check the configuration record: can we rebuild the same model from the same data snapshot, code version and seed? Finally I would ask an independent reviewer to look at the features and the metric choice for leakage, meaning information that would not be available at prediction time. If all of that holds, I would accept the result as a basis for the next step. The limit is that a peer review only checks what the reviewer thinks to look for, so a clean review does not prove the model will behave well on future data. That is why I would still plan monitoring after release.
rubricPoints: The test protocol and pass criteria must be fixed before the model is evaluated
The holdout test data must stay independent, not used for repeated tuning
Configuration records (data version, code, settings, seed) must allow the result to be reproduced
An independent peer review should check for leakage and an appropriate metric
A clean review does not guarantee future performance, so monitoring still matters

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers model QA protocols, so explaining the trust checks back to a teammate is the most direct practice for this objective.

lessons.plain: Training an AI model means repeatedly adjusting it on example data until it gets better at a task. Managing that training means deciding when each run happens and how much computing time it gets, choosing which settings to try, checking whether the model has truly learned something general rather than memorizing its examples, and keeping a written record of every attempt so results can be compared and repeated. Think of a coach running a season: they plan the practice schedule, try different drills, test players with scrimmages they have not rehearsed, and log every session so the team can see what actually worked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate's model scores 98 percent on the data it was trained on but only 71 percent on fresh data it has never seen. Before any teaching, what do you think went wrong, and what one habit would have caught the problem earlier?
lessons.teach:
A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training starts, such as how fast the model adjusts itself (the learning rate) or how complicated it is allowed to become (the tree depth). The training process does not learn these values from the data; people or search routines pick them. Cross-validation is a way to score a candidate setting honestly. You split the training data into equal groups called folds, train on all folds but one, score the model on the held-out fold, rotate which fold is held out, and average the scores. Experiment tracking is the running log of each run: the settings used, the data version, the code version, the scores, and when it ran. Scheduling is deciding the order and timing of those runs against your compute budget and deadlines.

Why it works: a score measured on data the model did not learn from estimates how it will behave on new data. Averaging over folds reduces the luck of any single split.

Worked example: you have 1,000 rows and try two learning rates with 5-fold cross-validation. Rate 0.1 scores 0.81, 0.79, 0.83, 0.80 and 0.82, averaging 0.81. Rate 0.01 scores 0.78, 0.80, 0.79, 0.78 and 0.80, averaging 0.79. You choose 0.1 and log both runs, the fold scores, and the data version.

Common mistake: tuning settings against the final test set until the score looks good. The test set is then no longer independent, and the reported score is too optimistic.

Consequence: a model that looks like 0.85 in the lab can fall to much lower accuracy in production, and nobody can explain why because the experiment history is missing.

A model is only as trustworthy as the honest, logged process that produced its settings.

questions.prompt: A retailer forecasting weekly demand has 800 rows and compares two tree depths using 4-fold cross-validation. Depth 6 gives fold scores 0.74, 0.71, 0.73 and 0.76, averaging 0.735. Depth 10 gives fold scores 0.70, 0.78, 0.69 and 0.73, averaging 0.725. The team picks depth 6 and logs both runs with their fold scores and the data version. Missing step: before anyone reports a final score, the team must ____.
choices: re-run cross-validation at depth 8 to see whether the average rises further
score the depth 6 model once on the untouched final test set and report that number
retrain on the final test set so the model sees all 800 rows before it is scored
average the two runs' fold scores together so one number represents the project
questions.why: The chosen setting is fixed first, then the final test set, which must stay independent of tuning, is used once to produce the reported score.

questions.prompt: A fraud team builds a k-nearest-neighbors model, where k is the number of neighboring transactions compared when making a prediction. Which of these is a hyperparameter?
choices: the value of k that the team sets before training starts
the date and time when the training job was launched
the transaction amount recorded for each row in the training data
the accuracy score the model achieves on the validation folds
questions.why: A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training rather than learned from the data, and k is set by the team before the run begins.

questions.prompt: A clinic's ML group tries 12 settings for a triage model. For each setting they score it on the same held-out set, keep the setting with the best score, and report that best score as the model's expected performance. Why is the reported number unreliable?
choices: The held-out set was used to choose the setting, so it is no longer independent and the score is too optimistic
Cross-validation was not used, so the scores cannot be averaged across folds
Twelve settings is too many, so the model overfits the training rows by default
The scores should be reported as a median rather than the best value
questions.why: Using the held-out set to select among settings makes it part of the tuning process, so the reported score overstates how the model will do on new data.

questions.prompt: A logistics company ran about 40 training runs over three weeks with limited GPU hours and a deadline in two weeks. Afterward, the best model fails on new shipments, and nobody can say which data version or learning rate produced it because no run records were kept. What is the gap?
choices: The company skipped cross-validation, so the scores were never averaged
The company should have used a larger fold count during scheduling
The company had no experiment tracking log of settings, data version, code version and scores for each run
The company scheduled too few runs against its compute budget
questions.why: Experiment tracking is the running record of each run's settings, data, code and scores, and without it the winning configuration cannot be reconstructed or explained.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we choose hyperparameters using cross-validation scores rather than scores on the training data. Name one limit or tradeoff of cross-validation.
lessons.modelAnswer: We use cross-validation scores because the training data is what the model has already studied, so its score there is flattering. Cross-validation holds out each fold in turn, so every score is measured on data the model did not learn from in that round. Averaging across folds gives a steadier estimate than a single split. The main limit is cost: if you train five folds for every candidate setting, a search over many settings multiplies compute time quickly, so teams limit the number of candidates or use a sensible schedule. There is also a subtler risk: if the folds ignore structure in the data, such as records from the same customer landing in both training and held-out folds, the scores will still look too good. Checking that the split matches real-world conditions is part of the job.
rubricPoints: Training-data scores overstate performance because the model has already seen that data.
Cross-validation scores each fold on data held out from that round of training, then averages.
A real tradeoff exists: more folds and more candidate settings cost more compute time.
The split must respect real structure, such as grouping related records, or the estimate is still biased.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine directly covers model training management, so an exam-style scenario to reason through best reinforces choosing the right tuning and evaluation step.

lessons.plain: Before a model can learn anything, the raw data usually needs work. Cleaning means fixing or removing bad entries, such as blanks, duplicates, and values that cannot be true. Feature engineering means building new, more useful input columns from existing ones, such as turning a timestamp into an hour of the day. Normalization, also called scaling, means putting numbers on comparable ranges so a column measured in thousands does not drown out one measured between zero and one. The project manager's job is to make sure every one of these steps is written down and can be repeated exactly, so the team and auditors can trust where the model's inputs came from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A loan dataset has an income column with some blank cells, and a credit score column that runs from 0 to 1. Before training, what would you want the team to do about the blanks, and why might it matter when they calculate the averages they use to fill those blanks?
lessons.teach:
Data preparation is the set of changes made to raw data before a model trains on it. Cleaning fixes or removes bad records: blanks, duplicates, and values that cannot be true, such as a negative vehicle speed. Feature engineering creates new input columns from existing ones, for example turning a timestamp into hour of day, because the model may find the derived signal easier to learn. Normalization, also called scaling, rescales numeric columns onto comparable ranges, since a column in the thousands would otherwise dominate one between zero and one. Reproducibility means anyone can rerun the same steps on the same raw data and get the same result. That requires recording the source data version, every rule applied, and every parameter used. A model only sees what preparation hands it, so any hidden step changes the results.

Worked example: a dataset has a monthly_spend column with blanks. Step 1: split the rows into training (80 percent) and test (20 percent). Step 2: compute the median of monthly_spend using only training rows, say 420. Step 3: fill blanks in both sets with 420. Step 4: compute the mean and standard deviation from training rows only, say 420 and 150, and scale both sets using those same two numbers. Step 5: write the cleaning rules, the source file version, and the random seed into the run log.

Common mistake: computing the median or scaling statistics on the full dataset before splitting. The test rows then influence the training inputs, a problem called data leakage, and the reported accuracy comes out higher than the model will achieve on new data.

Consequence: in production the model receives fresh records that must be scaled with the training numbers. If the team scales them with different numbers, predictions drift with no error raised, so the saved training statistics are part of the model.

questions.prompt: A parcel company in a fictional region is preparing data to predict late deliveries. Its raw file has a distance_km column with some blanks. The approved run log reads: Step 1: drop any row whose parcel ID appears a second time, keeping the first. Step 2: split the remaining rows into 70 percent training and 30 percent test. Step 3: compute the median of distance_km from training rows only, which is 11.5, and fill blanks in both sets with 11.5. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: write the file version, every rule, and the random seed into the run log. Which entry correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Scale the test rows using their own mean and standard deviation so each set is centred on its own average.
Compute the mean and standard deviation of distance_km from training rows only, then scale both sets using those two numbers.
Scale only the training rows, since the test rows are used only for the final score and need no changes.
Compute the mean and standard deviation of distance_km over all rows, then scale both sets with them so their ranges match.
questions.why: Scaling statistics must come from training rows only and be applied unchanged to both sets, so the test rows do not influence the training inputs and production can reuse the same numbers.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes reproducibility in data preparation?
choices: The trained model reaches the same accuracy on every new batch of incoming production data without any retraining.
All preparation code is stored in one file so that it runs faster on a new machine.
Anyone rerunning the same steps on the same raw data gets the same result, since the source version, rules, and parameters are recorded.
Every numeric column is converted to values between zero and one before any model is trained on it.
questions.why: Reproducibility means the same steps on the same raw data give the same result, which requires recording the source version, every rule, and every parameter.

questions.prompt: A bike-sharing dataset has a trip_minutes column containing a value of -4, plus a start_time column. Which pair of actions correctly separates cleaning from feature engineering?
choices: Derive start_hour from start_time to clean the -4, since the new column replaces the bad value.
Scale trip_minutes onto zero to one and keep the -4 so the model can learn from it.
Fix or remove the -4 as an impossible value; derive start_hour from start_time as a new input column.
Fill the -4 with the average of all trips, and scale start_time so its values are comparable.
questions.why: Cleaning removes or fixes values that cannot be true such as a negative trip duration, while feature engineering creates a new input column such as hour of day from an existing one.

questions.prompt: A fraud team computed the median of transaction_amount over all 500,000 rows before splitting into training and test sets. It reports 0.94 accuracy on test rows, but accuracy on new live transactions is 0.81. What is the most likely cause, and what should be done?
choices: The seed was recorded, so the gap must come from the model design; try a larger model with more layers.
The median fill was applied before scaling, so reverse the order of those two steps and report the same accuracy.
Test rows influenced the training inputs through the median computed on the full data; recompute the statistics from training rows only and rerun the pipeline.
Production records were scaled with the training numbers, so the drop reflects normal variation and needs no action.
questions.why: Computing preparation statistics before splitting leaks test information into training, which inflates reported accuracy; the fix is to compute statistics from training rows only and rerun.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should scale all features using the full dataset before splitting into training and test sets, since it is faster and gives the same numbers. Explain to them in your own words why this is risky, what you would ask the team to do instead, and one tradeoff of the approach you recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them the risk is leakage. If the scaling mean and standard deviation come from all rows, the test rows have already shaped the numbers the model trains on, so our test score looks better than the model really is. The fix is to split first, compute every statistic such as medians, means and standard deviations from training rows only, and then apply those same saved numbers to the test rows and to future live data. The tradeoff is that the approach needs a little more care: the team must store the fitted statistics with the model, and a new batch of data may fall outside the old range, which needs a documented rule. Those costs are small compared with reporting an inflated accuracy that the business then relies on.
rubricPoints: Explains that computing statistics on all data before splitting leaks test information into training
Says to split first and fit cleaning and scaling statistics on training rows only
Notes that the same saved statistics must be applied to test and future data
States a real tradeoff such as storing fitted parameters or handling out-of-range values

suggested.rationale: A scenario where a team proposes a preparation shortcut lets the learner reason through the leakage risk, which adds more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Before a computer learns anything from data, someone has to check whether that data is fit for the job. A go/no-go decision is a yes-or-no call at a checkpoint: go means the data is good enough to start training, and no-go means stop and fix it first. The same kind of check happens again later, before a trained model is handed to the people and systems that will run it for real. At that point the question is whether the model is ready to work in the real world, not just whether it scored well in a lab. A project manager makes sure these checkpoints happen, that they have clear criteria, and that the right people sign off.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has 500,000 customer records to train a model that predicts late deliveries, but 30 percent of the delivery dates are blank and nobody knows whether the blanks are random. Should the project start training now, and what single fact would you want to know first?
lessons.teach:
A data readiness check is a structured review of training data against written criteria, ending in a go/no-go decision. Go means the data meets the agreed bar and training can start. No-go means work stops until the named problems are fixed. The main quality dimensions to check are completeness (how much of the data is present), accuracy (whether values are correct), consistency (whether the same thing is recorded the same way across sources), timeliness (whether the data is recent enough for the real situation), and representativeness (whether the data covers the cases the model will meet in use). When examples carry labels, meaning the correct answer attached to each example, label quality is checked too.

Why this matters: a model can only learn patterns present in its training data, so flawed or unrepresentative data produces a model that looks fine in testing and fails in the field.

Worked example, a late-delivery predictor. Step 1: measure completeness and find 30 percent of delivery dates blank. Step 2: check whether the blanks cluster, and find most sit in one region. Step 3: compare against the agreed criteria, which allow at most 10 percent missing with no regional clustering. Step 4: record a no-go, backfill the dates from the carrier system, and run the checks again before deciding.

Common mistake: treating the go decision as a one-time event at project start. Data sources change, so the check must repeat whenever the source, pipeline, or time window changes.

Model readiness for operationalization is a second gate, held before a trained model goes live. Confirm it meets the success criteria on a test set it never trained on, that performance holds for important segments, that results can be reproduced from recorded settings, that its latency and inputs fit production, and that monitoring and a rollback path exist. Each gate needs a named approver.

Consequence in a running system: a model trained on the skewed data would underpredict lateness for one region, and dispatchers would trust forecasts that are systematically wrong there. A passed gate is only as good as the criteria behind it.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer wants a model to flag claims likely to be disputed, and its training set holds 4,000 past claims. A label is the correct answer attached to each example, here whether a claim was disputed. Step 1: measure completeness and find 6 percent of claim amounts blank. Step 2: check whether the blanks cluster, and find nearly all sit in one branch office. Step 3: check label quality by having a second adjuster re-label 200 claims, and find 26 disagree. Step 4 is missing. The agreed criteria allow at most 10 percent missing with no clustering, and at most 5 percent label disagreement. Which completion correctly supplies the missing final step?
choices: Record a go, because the missing amounts are under the 10 percent limit and training can start.
Record a no-go, naming both failed criteria, and re-run the checks after the fixes.
Record a go and fix the labels during training, since the model can learn around some noise.
Record a no-go and skip the re-run, since the fixes only add rows to the data.
questions.why: The check ends with a go or no-go decision against the written criteria, and here the clustered blanks and the 13 percent label disagreement both fail, so the correct completion is a no-go that names those failures and repeats the checks after fixes.

questions.prompt: A logistics team's training data covers only one peak season of shipments, but the model will forecast demand all year. Which quality dimension does this gap fail?
choices: Accuracy, because the shipment counts may be wrong in the peak months.
Consistency, because the season was recorded in a different format from other years.
Completeness, because some months have fewer recorded shipments than others.
Representativeness, because the data does not cover the cases the model will meet in use.
questions.why: Representativeness asks whether the training data covers the cases the model will meet in use, and a single season leaves out much of the year, while the other options describe different dimensions.

questions.prompt: A team asks whether a model is ready to go live because it scored very high on the examples it was trained on. Which readiness gate has been skipped?
choices: Reproducibility from recorded settings, since the training run was not logged.
Evaluation on a test set the model never trained on, since high training scores do not show it generalises.
Monitoring and rollback, since the model has no live dashboard yet.
Latency and input fit, since the training speed was never measured.
questions.why: A model judged on examples it trained on can look accurate by memorising them, so the readiness gate requires confirming success criteria on a held-out test set before go-live.

questions.prompt: A support team has 2,000 labeled tickets. A second reviewer re-labels a random sample of 150 and disagrees with the original label on 22 of them. What is the most appropriate response under a data readiness check?
choices: Delete the 22 disagreeing tickets and treat the remaining labels as correct.
Assume the disagreements average out during training, so no action is needed.
Treat label quality as a failed check if disagreement exceeds the agreed bar, and decide go or no-go against the criteria.
Re-label the full set with a single reviewer, since one reviewer is always consistent.
questions.why: Label quality is a named part of a readiness check, and 22 disagreements in 150 (about 15 percent) must be judged against the agreed bar rather than assumed to cancel out or fixed by a quiet deletion.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who will sit on the go/no-go review what the decision checks for in training data, and name one limit of a data check: what passing it does not guarantee.
lessons.modelAnswer: A go/no-go on training data is a checkpoint where we compare the data against criteria we wrote down in advance: how complete it is, whether values are accurate and consistent, whether it is recent enough, whether it represents the cases the model will see, and whether labels are reliable. If it passes, training starts; if not, we stop, fix the named gaps, and check again. The limit is that passing shows the data meets the checklist, not that the model will be good. A clean dataset can still miss rare situations or drift after launch. So the same discipline applies to the model before it goes live: test on unseen data, check important segments, confirm results can be reproduced, and make sure monitoring and a rollback plan exist before anyone approves operation.
rubricPoints: Names the data criteria checked, such as completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, representativeness and label quality.
Explains that go means training starts and no-go means stopping to fix named gaps, then rechecking.
States that a passing data check does not guarantee model quality or coverage of rare cases.
Notes that model readiness needs unseen test data, segment checks, reproducibility, and monitoring with a rollback plan before operation.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises go/no-go gates, so an exam-style situation to reason through, using the criteria from this lesson, adds the most.

lessons.plain: A deployment plan is the written agreement for how an AI model moves from testing into real use. It states which rollout approach the team will take, what dates and checkpoints it will hit, what servers, data feeds and monitoring the model needs, and exactly how the team will return to the previous working version if the new one misbehaves. Think of it like moving a restaurant to a new kitchen: you decide how customers switch over, when, what equipment must be installed first, and what you do if the first night goes badly. Without the plan, the team improvises under pressure.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new model version is ready and the old one is still running. Before any teaching, what would you want written down in advance so that switching back takes minutes rather than a day?
lessons.teach:
A deployment plan is a document that answers four questions before anything goes live. First, the strategy: how traffic moves from the old version to the new one. A big-bang switch sends everything at once. A canary release sends a small share of traffic, say 5 percent, to the new version first and widens it only while measurements stay healthy. A shadow deployment runs the new model on real inputs while its outputs are hidden from users, so the team can compare results without risk. Second, the timeline: dated gates, each with an entry condition such as accuracy on a holdout set above an agreed threshold, and a named owner who signs off. Third, infrastructure requirements: the compute the model needs at peak load, the data pipelines that feed it, the exact feature-data version, logging, and the monitoring that will detect drift. Fourth, rollback procedures: the trigger that starts a rollback, the exact steps to restore the previous model version and its configuration, who authorizes it, and how long it should take.

Why it works: a rollback is only fast if the old version was kept deployable and the switch was rehearsed. Each stage limits how many users a bad model can harm before someone notices.

Worked example: a credit-scoring model version 2 is ready. The plan sends 5 percent of applications to version 2 for one week. Gate: the approval rate differs from version 1 by less than 3 points, and no fairness alert fires. On day 4 the fairness alert fires. The trigger says roll back if it fires twice within 24 hours. It fires a second time, the on-call lead authorizes, and traffic returns to version 1 within 10 minutes, because version 1 was still running and its configuration was tagged.

Common mistake: writing the rollback step as revert the model, with no tested path, and then discovering that version 1 cannot run because the input data schema has changed. Consequence: a model that cannot be rolled back forces the team to keep serving a harmful version while they rebuild.

A deployment plan is only trustworthy when its rollback path has been rehearsed before launch.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain has a demand-forecast model. Version 3 is ready to replace version 2. The deployment plan sends 10 percent of stores to version 3 for six days. Gate on day six: weekly forecast error across the canary stores is no more than 2 percentage points worse than version 2, and the named inventory owner signs off. Rollback trigger: if the error gap exceeds 2 points on two consecutive days, roll back. On day five the gap is 3 points on day four and 3 points on day five, so the trigger fires and the team starts a rollback. The plan has one missing step, the one that makes this restore fast and dependable. Which step must be added before launch?
choices: Delete version 2's model files once version 3 passes its day-six gate, to free storage.
Ask the model's developer to confirm version 3's error rate in writing before the canary starts.
Rehearse the rollback: restore version 2 with its tagged configuration on a copy of the current pipeline before launch, and confirm it runs.
Raise the canary share to 50 percent on day three so the team collects more error data sooner.
questions.why: A rollback is only fast when the old version has been kept deployable and the switch has been rehearsed before launch, so the rehearsal is the missing step.

questions.prompt: A payments company wants to test a new fraud-scoring model against live transactions without any risk to customers. The new model scores every real transaction, but its scores are logged and never acted on. Which deployment strategy is this?
choices: Big-bang switch, because all transactions move to the new model at once.
Canary release, because a small share of live traffic is sent to the new model.
Shadow deployment, because the new model runs on real inputs while its outputs stay hidden from customers.
Rollback-first release, because the old model is kept as a fallback.
questions.why: A shadow deployment runs the new model on real inputs with its outputs hidden, which is exactly what the payments company describes.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket triage model, version 4, is being prepared to replace version 3. The team says a rollback would be fast because they will just switch the model back if needed. Which condition most determines whether that rollback will actually be fast?
choices: Whether the company's support staff have been told about the change in advance.
Whether the team wrote a longer description of version 4's improvements.
Whether version 4 has a larger number of features than version 3.
Whether version 3 was kept deployable with its configuration tagged, and the switch back was rehearsed before launch.
questions.why: A rollback is fast only when the old version was kept deployable and the switch was rehearsed, so the existence of a tagged, runnable version 3 and a rehearsal decide speed.

questions.prompt: A retail pricing model has a timeline with a gate before traffic increases from 5 percent to 25 percent. Which gate is written well enough to use in the plan?
choices: The gate opens when the vendor's contract for the model is renewed.
The gate opens if no one objects to the wider rollout by Friday afternoon.
The gate opens when the team feels confident the model is ready for wider use.
The gate opens once holdout accuracy is above the agreed threshold of 0.88 and the named pricing owner has signed off, dated for week two.
questions.why: A usable gate has a dated checkpoint, an entry condition measured against an agreed threshold, and a named owner who signs off, which only the second choice provides.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who will run the first canary release of a new AI model: what must be written into the deployment plan before launch, and what limit or tradeoff a canary release introduces.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before launch, the plan needs a chosen strategy, here a canary at a small traffic share, plus dated gates with entry conditions and named owners. It must list the infrastructure the model needs at peak load, the data pipelines and feature versions it depends on, and the monitoring that will catch drift or fairness problems. The rollback section needs explicit triggers, such as a sustained error rate or a fairness alert, the exact steps to restore the previous version and its configuration, and who can authorize the switch. The main tradeoff of a canary is that only a fraction of users see the new model, so rare failures or slow-building drift may not appear in the sample. The canary also takes longer than a big-bang switch, and the team must keep two versions running during that time, which costs extra compute.
rubricPoints: Names the deployment strategy and explains what it does in plain terms
Lists the timeline gates with entry conditions and owners
Covers infrastructure needs including data dependencies and monitoring
Defines rollback triggers, steps and authority, and notes it must be rehearsed
States a real tradeoff such as limited sample size or the cost of running two versions

suggested.rationale: Comparing canary, shadow and big-bang strategies and their rollback triggers is best practised in the planned deployment-strategies engine.

lessons.plain: Putting an AI model into real use is more than switching it on. Several people and systems have to start working together at the same time, and then someone has to check that the model actually behaves well with real data, real users, and real load, not just the test data it was built on. This objective is about that coordination and checking: deciding how the new model goes live, confirming it performs as promised once it is live, and running a set of verification checks after launch to catch problems early. Think of it like opening a new kitchen: the chef, suppliers, and front desk all need to be ready, and the first orders get watched closely before the kitchen is trusted with a full dinner rush.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank's new loan-approval model passed every test on last year's data. On launch day, what is the single most important thing the team should check before sending it all applications, and why?
lessons.teach:
Deployment coordination means arranging the people, systems, and timing so a model moves from a test environment into production, the live setting where real users and real decisions depend on it. Production performance validation means measuring the live model against agreed targets, such as accuracy or error rate, response time, and rejected-input rate, using real traffic rather than the historical test set. Post-deployment verification is the set of checks run after go-live to confirm the model, its inputs, and its surrounding services work as intended. A baseline is the reference measurement, usually taken from the previous model or from test results, that live numbers are compared against. A canary release sends a small share of traffic, for example five percent, to the new model while the rest still goes to the old one. A rollback trigger is a threshold agreed in advance, which, when crossed, sends traffic back to the previous model.

Why this works: a small live sample reveals problems that offline tests miss, such as messy inputs, changed user behavior, or slower responses, while limiting the damage if the model is wrong. The team decides the thresholds before launch so nobody argues about them under pressure.

Worked example: a demand-forecast model is set to replace the current one. Step 1: record the baseline error of the current model over the last 30 days. Step 2: route five percent of traffic to the new model for 48 hours. Step 3: compare the new model's error on that slice with the baseline, and check latency and the count of rejected inputs. Step 4: error is within the agreed tolerance and latency is normal, so the team widens traffic to 50 percent. Step 5: after a week of stable numbers, the old model is retired and the verification checklist is signed off.

Common mistake: declaring success because the launch did not crash. A model can run without errors and still give worse predictions. In a running system, a silently degraded model keeps producing poor outputs that downstream systems act on, often for days before anyone notices, so validation must measure prediction quality, not just uptime.

questions.prompt: A fraud-alert model at a regional bank is being phased in. The team followed the sequence below, but one step is missing. Step 1: the current model's false-positive rate (alerts raised on legitimate card payments) was 2.1 percent over the last 60 days, which serves as the baseline. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: send 10 percent of card transactions to the new model for 72 hours. Step 4: the new model's false-positive rate on that slice was 2.3 percent, inside the agreed 0.5-point tolerance, so the team moved to 40 percent of traffic. Which action fills the gap at Step 2?
choices: Agree a rollback trigger in advance, such as a false-positive rate above 3.0 percent over 24 hours sending traffic back to the old model
Switch off logging of the old model so the live system runs faster
Tell the fraud analysts the new model is live so they can watch the alert queue
Retrain the new model on the 72-hour slice before any live traffic is sent
questions.why: A rollback trigger is a threshold agreed before launch so the team is not arguing about it under pressure, and it has to be set before the canary traffic starts, which is why it belongs at Step 2.

questions.prompt: An invoice-classification model at a mid-sized accounts payable firm is ready for live traffic. Its team wants to judge how well it performs in production. Which reference number should the live error be compared against?
choices: The error of the current model measured over a recent period before the switch
The vendor's published accuracy figure for similar models
The rollback trigger value the team wrote down before launch
The server's average CPU usage during the launch hour
questions.why: A baseline is the reference measurement, taken from the previous model or from test results, that live numbers are compared against, whereas a rollback trigger is a threshold rather than a reference measurement.

questions.prompt: A ranking model for a streaming service's home page went live. For five days the service logged no errors, and the team declared the launch a success. Only after that did the team set its rollback threshold, using day-one numbers. Which statement best names the flaw?
choices: Five days is too short to ever declare a deployment successful, so the team should have waited for a full quarter before judging anything at all
Error-free logs prove the model is accurate, so a rollback threshold was never needed in the first place
The team judged the launch on error-free running rather than prediction quality, and it should have agreed its rollback thresholds before launch
A rollback threshold is only useful when the model crashes outright, so setting one from day-one numbers was harmless
questions.why: A model can run without errors while giving worse predictions, so validation must measure prediction quality, and rollback thresholds must be fixed before launch so they are not set under pressure.

questions.prompt: A warehouse route-planning model is in a 5 percent canary. The team agreed before launch that a sustained response time above 300 milliseconds triggers rollback. After 48 hours, the new model's routing error is within tolerance, but its response time has stayed around 400 milliseconds. What should the team do?
choices: Wait one more week and check whether response time falls on its own
Retrain the model on the canary data, then restart the canary from zero traffic and watch response time again
Widen traffic to 50 percent, because the error measure is within tolerance and the other numbers can be reviewed later
Route the canary traffic back to the old model, because the agreed latency trigger has been crossed even though error is acceptable
questions.why: A rollback trigger is a threshold agreed in advance, and when it is crossed traffic goes back to the previous model, so the pre-agreed latency limit being exceeded means rollback regardless of the error result.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to AI projects how we decide that a newly deployed model is performing well in production, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: We do not decide that from the launch being quiet. Before the release we agree on the baseline the old model achieved and on the thresholds that matter: error or accuracy on live traffic, response time, and the rate of rejected inputs. Then we send a small share of real traffic to the new model, a canary, and compare its live numbers with the baseline over a set window, such as 48 hours. If it stays within tolerance, we widen the share in steps; if any threshold is crossed, we roll back to the old model. After go-live we run post-deployment checks, such as confirming that monitoring and logging are receiving data and that outputs look sensible on a sample of cases. The tradeoff is that a small canary has limited statistical power: rare failures or slow drift may not show up in 48 hours, so verification has to continue after full rollout.
rubricPoints: Defines a baseline and agreed thresholds before the release, not after
Uses a staged rollout such as a canary with a clear rollback trigger
Measures prediction quality and latency on live traffic, not just whether the system is up
Names a real limit, such as small samples missing rare failures or slow drift, and says verification continues after rollout

suggested.rationale: A deployment-strategies engine would let the learner run canary and staged rollouts against a baseline and choose when to roll back, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Model governance is the set of rules and records that keep an AI model under control after it is built. It covers the model's whole life, from the first trial version to the day it is retired. Versioning gives every trained model its own numbered record, so anyone can tell which model made a given prediction and go back to an earlier one if needed. Drift detection means watching the model after release, because the real world changes and a model trained on last year's situations can quietly get worse. Think of it as a logbook with a serial number on every copy and a regular check that the machine still does its job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A demand-forecasting model was approved and released six months ago and has been running without any complaints. Someone suggests it needs no further checks until its next scheduled rebuild. Would you agree, and what could go wrong in the meantime?
lessons.teach: Model governance is the set of controls that oversee an AI model across its lifecycle, meaning the stages it passes through from idea and training to release, monitoring and retirement. Each stage can have a gate, which is a named approval that someone must sign before the model moves on. Versioning means giving each trained model a unique identifier, such as version 3.2, and recording with it the training data snapshot, the code, the settings and the evaluation results. This linked record is called lineage. Without lineage you cannot say which model produced yesterday's predictions or what changed between two versions. Drift is change over time that makes a model less accurate. Data drift means the inputs look different from the training data, for example customers now ordering in different quantities. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the correct answer has changed, even when the inputs look similar. Drift detection compares live inputs and outcomes against a baseline captured at release, and raises an alert when the gap passes an agreed threshold. Worked example: a demand-forecast model, version 3.2, was trained on 2023 sales. Step 1: weekly monitoring finds the average order size has risen 40 percent. Step 2: the drift score crosses the threshold agreed at approval. Step 3: the alert opens a review ticket. Step 4: the approvers check accuracy against recent actual sales, confirm it has dropped, and either retrain through the approval gate to version 3.3 or roll back to 3.1, the last approved version that was still accurate. Common mistake: treating a passing launch test as proof the model stays fine, and therefore monitoring nothing. In a running system this means forecasts stay confident while wrong, orders are placed on bad numbers, and nobody can tell which version caused the damage because no lineage was kept. Governance is therefore an ongoing cycle of recording, watching and deciding, not a one-time sign-off.

questions.prompt: A card-payment fraud model, version 5.0, was trained on 2022 transactions and its live scores are checked weekly against a baseline captured at release. Step 1: monitoring shows the share of online card-not-present payments has risen from 30 percent to 55 percent. Step 2: the drift score crosses the threshold agreed at approval, and an alert opens a review ticket. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: approvers check the catch rate on recent confirmed fraud cases, find it fell from 88 percent to 61 percent, and decide to retrain through the approval gate as version 5.1, since the last approved version has also lost accuracy on current traffic. Which action belongs in the blank Step 3?
choices: Retire version 5.0 immediately and switch all live traffic to an untested newly trained model without any review by the approvers.
Delete the 2022 training data so the team starts clean before any retraining.
Raise the drift threshold so future alerts stop firing on this change in payment mix.
Pull the lineage record for version 5.0 to confirm which data, code and settings produced the live scores.
questions.why: Lineage is the linked record of training snapshot, code, settings and evaluation for a version, and checking it before the approval decision establishes exactly what produced the live scores.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling model predicts which appointments will be missed. Since release, the age mix of patients has shifted toward older adults, but the relationship between age, distance and missed appointments is unchanged. Which kind of drift is this, and why?
choices: Data drift: the inputs look different from the training data, but the input-to-outcome relationship is unchanged.
Concept drift, since any change in inputs always changes what the correct answer is for them.
Neither, because drift only happens when the model's code is edited after release.
Concept drift, since the correct answer for each patient must now differ from what the model learned.
questions.why: Data drift means the inputs shift while the link between inputs and correct answers stays the same, which matches this case.

questions.prompt: A credit-scoring team retrains its model and overwrites the saved files of version 2.1 with the new weights, keeping no record of the training data snapshot or settings used for 2.1. Three months later a regulator asks which model produced a set of past decisions. What is the core problem?
choices: The model's accuracy must have fallen, so the past decisions are automatically invalid.
The team has too few versions, so it should have kept at least five active models at once.
Lineage was lost, so the team cannot reliably tie those past decisions to the exact model that made them.
Nothing is wrong, because a version number alone is enough to recover any past model.
questions.why: Without lineage linking each version to its data, code and settings, you cannot say which model produced a given output or what changed between versions.

questions.prompt: A churn model was released with a baseline accuracy of 0.82. The agreed drift threshold is an accuracy drop of more than 0.05 from baseline. Current accuracy is 0.76. What should happen?
choices: No alert, because 0.76 is still above 0.75 and the gap is within what most teams accept.
No alert, because accuracy only counts as dropped when it falls below 0.5.
An alert opens, because the drop of 0.06 is larger than the agreed 0.05 threshold.
An alert opens only if the drop reaches 0.10, since that is the usual limit.
questions.why: The drop from 0.82 to 0.76 is 0.06, which exceeds the agreed 0.05 threshold, so drift detection should raise an alert and open a review.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked with AI models what model governance covers, including versioning and drift detection. Name one limit or tradeoff of drift monitoring.
lessons.modelAnswer: Model governance is the control layer around an AI model after it is built: who approves each release, which version is live, and whether it still performs as expected. Versioning means each trained model gets a unique number with a lineage record of its data, code and settings, so we can answer which model made a prediction and roll back to a known-good version. Drift detection watches live inputs and outcomes against a baseline from release and alerts when the gap passes an agreed threshold. The main tradeoff is sensitivity. A tight threshold catches real degradation early but produces false alarms that waste review time, while a loose one lets the model drift for weeks. Also, a drift alert shows that something changed, not why, or whether accuracy actually fell, so someone must still check recent outcomes before retraining or rolling back.
rubricPoints: Defines model governance as controls across the model lifecycle, including approval gates
Explains versioning with lineage so a prediction can be traced to its model and data
Distinguishes drift detection as comparing live data against a release baseline with a threshold
Names a concrete tradeoff, such as false alarms versus late detection, or that an alert is not proof of accuracy loss

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining governance controls and their tradeoffs back in plain words, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model lifecycle governance directly.

lessons.plain: Once an AI system is running, someone has to keep checking that it still does its job. Overseeing metrics means choosing a small set of numbers that show how healthy the system is, putting them on a dashboard people actually look at, comparing them with targets over time, and getting an alert when a number slides past a line agreed in advance. Think of a car dashboard: speed alone tells you little, but fuel, engine temperature and warning lights together tell you when something is going wrong. For an AI system, the numbers cover both technical behaviour and whether the system still helps the business.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fraud-scoring model scored very well in testing. Six months after launch it misses more fraud, but nobody was alerted. What one kind of change would have caught this earlier, and why would watching only one number not be enough?
lessons.teach:
A KPI (key performance indicator) is a number tied to a goal, such as fraud losses prevented per month. A model metric is a measure of the model itself, such as recall, the share of real fraud cases the model catches. A baseline is the value measured while the system was healthy, and it is the reference point for judging change. A threshold is the line that triggers an alert. Degradation is a gradual loss of quality after launch. Drift is a shift in the incoming data away from what the model learned from. Ground truth lag is the delay before the correct answer becomes known, which can hide degradation for weeks.

Why it works: a number compared with its own baseline and a pre-agreed line shows change early, while a dashboard nobody watches shows nothing.

Worked example: in the first month a fraud model has a 7-day recall baseline of 0.80. The team sets an alert for when recall stays below 0.72 for three days in a row. In week ten recall falls to 0.70 on three consecutive days, so the alert fires. A drift check on the same week shows that the merchant mix has changed, which explains the drop and points to retraining.

Common mistake: watching only server uptime or offline test accuracy. The service answers every request with a success code while its predictions quietly decay.

Consequence: without a model-level threshold, losses accumulate for weeks before anyone asks whether the system still works.

A well-run AI system pairs business KPIs with model metrics, sets baselines before launch, and alerts on sustained movement past agreed thresholds.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer deploys a model that sorts incoming claims into fast-track or manual review. In the first week after launch, its 7-day precision baseline (the share of fast-tracked claims that really qualify) is 0.91. The team sets an alert to fire when precision stays below 0.85 for four days in a row. In week six, precision is 0.84 on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. A drift check shows the share of claims written in a language the model rarely saw in training has risen sharply. Step one is done: 0.84 is below the 0.85 line on each of four consecutive days, which matches the alert rule. Step two is missing: what should the team conclude about the alert?
choices: The alert fires only after the ground-truth lag of the claims is over, so the team must wait for confirmed outcomes first.
The alert fires, because the sustained run past the agreed threshold matches the rule the team set in advance.
The alert does not fire, because 0.84 is only a hair under the line and single-point dips are normal.
The alert fires, but only because precision fell by 0.07 from baseline, not because of the threshold rule.
questions.why: The alert rule is a pre-agreed threshold held for a set number of consecutive days, and four days below 0.85 meets that rule regardless of the drift check or label delay.

questions.prompt: A warehouse demand-forecasting team tracks two numbers: stockout hours avoided per week, and the mean percentage error of the forecast against actual sales. Which statement correctly classifies them?
choices: Stockout hours avoided is a KPI tied to a business goal, and forecast error is a model metric measuring the model itself.
Both are model metrics, because both are computed from the forecast output.
Both are KPIs, because any number the team watches on a dashboard counts as a KPI.
Stockout hours avoided is a model metric, and forecast error is a KPI, because the model's error is the business outcome.
questions.why: A KPI is a number tied to a business goal, while a model metric measures the model itself, so stockout hours map to the goal and forecast error measures the model.

questions.prompt: A support chatbot's deflection rate (share of conversations resolved without a human agent) was 0.62 in the first month, and that value was recorded as the baseline. Human-verified answer quality is only known about 30 days after each conversation. Which alerting setup best fits this situation?
choices: Wait for the 30-day verified quality scores before setting any alert, since nothing can be judged earlier.
Alert whenever a single conversation receives a low satisfaction rating, since one bad case signals degradation.
Set the alert threshold at 0.62 exactly, so any single day below the first-month value fires an alarm.
Alert on deflection rate falling below the agreed line for several days in a row, while tracking input drift from the start.
questions.why: Because ground-truth labels arrive late, the team should watch a timely proxy KPI against its baseline with a sustained-movement threshold and check input drift while waiting for verified results.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's route-scoring model runs on a managed endpoint. The operations dashboard shows 99.98% uptime and every request returns a success code, yet dispatchers report more bad routes each week. Which gap best explains the situation?
choices: The team set the uptime baseline too high, so the alert threshold never fires.
The endpoint is too slow, so requests time out before the model can produce its routes.
The dashboard tracks service health but not model-level quality, so the decay in predictions goes unnoticed.
Uptime was measured on a test server rather than production, so the reported numbers are invalid.
questions.why: Uptime and success codes show the service is answering, but they say nothing about whether the predictions are still good, which requires model-level metrics compared with a baseline.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why an AI system needs both business KPIs and model-level metrics on its monitoring dashboard, and name one limit or tradeoff of setting alert thresholds.
lessons.modelAnswer: Business KPIs such as fraud losses or order throughput tell us whether the system is still worth running. Model metrics such as recall or precision tell us whether the model itself is still behaving as it did when it was approved. Either one alone can mislead. A service can be up and returning answers while its predictions get worse, and business numbers often move for reasons unrelated to the model. The tradeoff is with thresholds. Set them too tight and the team gets constant false alarms and starts ignoring the dashboard. Set them too loose and real degradation goes unnoticed until losses are large. Thresholds should be set against a baseline measured while the system was healthy, and they should be reviewed as data and business conditions change.
rubricPoints: Business KPIs show whether the system still delivers value
Model metrics show whether the model itself is still performing as approved
A baseline and an agreed threshold give the alert a meaningful reference
Tight thresholds cause alert fatigue and loose ones miss real degradation

suggested.rationale: The metric alarm builder planned for OpsForge would let the learner set baselines and thresholds and see when an alert fires, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When an AI project finishes building a model and moves it into real use, two things must be written down and handed over. The final report is the record of what was built, how well it performed, what limits it has, and what decisions were made along the way. The lessons learned are an honest list of what went well, what went wrong, and what the next team should do differently. The transition plan is the agreed handover of day-to-day ownership to the people who will run and support the system after the project team leaves. It is like moving into a house: the previous owner leaves a folder of manuals, known quirks, and a clear note of who fixes what when something breaks.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project team has finished building an AI model that works well in testing, and the project manager is about to disband the team. What is the most likely thing to go wrong in the weeks after launch, and what written handover would have prevented it?
lessons.teach:
The final report is a written summary of the finished AI solution: its purpose, the data it was trained on and that data's known gaps, the performance measured against the targets agreed earlier, the conditions where it is weak, and the decisions taken and why. Lessons learned is a short, candid review of what helped and hurt the project, written so the next team does not repeat the same mistakes. The transition plan is the agreed hand-over of ownership to the operational or production support team, the group that keeps a live system running and answers incidents. Production support means the people on call when the system misbehaves at night.

It works because knowledge about a model lives partly in people's heads. Support staff cannot fix what they do not understand, and they cannot judge whether a strange result is a bug or expected behaviour without the context that the report provides.

Worked example: a churn-prediction model. Step 1: the report records that it was trained on 18 months of customer data, targeted 80 percent accuracy on held-out data, and reached 83 percent, but is weaker for customers with under three months of history. Step 2: the lessons learned notes that a late change to the data feed cost two weeks, and recommends checking the feed's structure before each training run. Step 3: the transition plan names the operations team as owner of the scoring job, the data science lead as second-line contact for model questions, the alert thresholds support will watch, and a sign-off date when operations has run the system without project staff.

Common mistake: writing the report after the team has gone, or treating the handover as a single email. When the scoring job fails at 2 a.m., on-call staff cannot tell whether a drop in predictions is a fault or expected behaviour for new customers, so they either ignore it or roll back without knowing why.

A handover is complete only when the operations team can handle the next incident using the documents alone.

questions.prompt: A regional grocery chain builds a model that flags produce likely to spoil, for its 40 stores. The team trained it on 14 months of sales and waste logs and set a target of 75 percent recall on held-out weeks. The final report records that the model reached 78 percent recall and is weaker for stores that opened less than four months ago. The lessons learned notes that a supplier changed its product barcode codes mid-project and cost three weeks, and recommends checking the code mapping before each training run. Step 3, which the learner must complete: the transition plan is written for the operations team. Which entry correctly completes it?
choices: Delivery of the report and a single handover email to the store operations manager, with the project closed the same day

Named owner of the nightly flagging job, a second-line contact for model questions, the alert thresholds support will watch, and a sign-off date after operations has run the system without project staff
Deletion of the training logs once the model is live, to reduce storage costs for the operations team
A quarterly retraining schedule owned by the data science team, with no named operations owner
questions.why: The transition plan must name the operational owner, the second-line model contact, the alert thresholds to watch, and a sign-off date after operations runs the system alone, which is what lets the team handle incidents from the documents.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the purpose of a lessons learned review in an AI project?
choices: A list of every technical decision the team made, with no judgement about which ones worked
A formal record of the model's accuracy figures, kept so auditors can verify the final score
A short, candid review of what helped and hurt the project, written so the next team does not repeat the same mistakes
A forecast of the model's accuracy over the next three years of operation
questions.why: Lessons learned is defined in the teaching text as a candid review of what helped and hurt, written to prevent the next team from repeating mistakes, not as a score record or a forecast.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency builds a model that predicts bus delays. Its testing showed the model was much less accurate during snowstorms, because few snowstorm days were in the training data. Which item should appear in the final report, and where?
choices: No mention at all, since the snowstorm days were a small share of the total
A note in the conditions-where-it-is-weak section that the model is less accurate during snowstorms, because of the thin training data for those days
A line in the lessons learned saying the snow data was hard to get, with no mention of the model's accuracy
A claim in the performance section that the model met its target on all days, including snowstorms
questions.why: The final report must record the conditions where the model is weak and the known data gaps behind them, so support staff can judge whether poor snowstorm predictions are a fault or expected behaviour.
