questions.prompt: A payments company hands its fraud-scoring model to the on-call team with only a single email and no final report. At 1 a.m. the team sees approval scores drop sharply for one new customer segment. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The team immediately retrains the model on the new segment, which fixes the drop before anyone checks the cause
The problem is reported to the data science lead, who answers within minutes and clears the incident
The scores recover by themselves in the morning, so the missing report causes no harm
The team has no way to know the drop is expected for new customers, so it either ignores a real fault or rolls back without knowing why
questions.why: Without the report, on-call staff lack the context to separate a fault from expected behaviour, so they either ignore the drop or roll back blindly, which is the common handover failure the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is about to take over support of a newly launched AI model what the final report and transition plan must contain before ownership moves. Name one limit or tradeoff of writing these documents at the end of the project rather than during it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The final report should state what the model is for, the data it was trained on and that data's known gaps, the performance measured against the agreed targets, the conditions where it is weak, and the decisions made and why. The transition plan should name each owner, the on-call route, the alerts the support team will watch, the runbook for common failures, and a sign-off date when operations has run the system without project staff. The tradeoff is that writing at the end is cheaper during the build but risks losing detail: people forget why choices were made, and the lessons learned become shallow. Keeping a running decision log during the project and polishing it at the end reduces that risk, though it costs some time while the team is busy delivering.
rubricPoints: The final report covers purpose, training data and its gaps, measured performance against targets, and known weak conditions.
The transition plan names owners, the on-call route, the alerts support will watch, and the runbook for common failures.
Handover is confirmed by a sign-off, ideally after operations has run the system without project staff.
Names a real limit, such as detail being lost when documents are written only at the end, and a way to mitigate it.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the handover back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or engine practises writing a report or transition plan.

lessons.plain: A contingency plan is the set of written steps a team follows when an AI system fails, goes down, or behaves badly. It answers three questions before anything breaks: how do we notice and contain a problem quickly (incident response), how do we bring the system back if a whole site or data store is lost (disaster recovery), and how does the business keep working in the meantime (business continuity). Think of it like a fire drill in a restaurant kitchen: nobody hopes to use it, but everyone knows where the exits and extinguishers are before the smoke starts.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI scoring service starts producing obviously wrong outputs at 2 a.m., and the on-call engineer is alone. Before you read anything else, what would you want that engineer to do first, and what would you want them to avoid doing?
lessons.teach:
Incident response is the process of detecting a problem, containing its damage, communicating, finding the cause, and recording what was learned. A runbook is a written, step-by-step procedure for one kind of failure, so the on-call person does not have to invent steps under pressure. Disaster recovery (DR) is the process of restoring a system after a major loss, such as a failed data centre or deleted data. Two targets drive DR design. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest acceptable time to be back up. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. Business continuity means keeping the business function running during the outage, often through a fallback such as a simpler rule-based process or a manual review queue.

Worked example: a fraud model approves card payments. At 02:10 a monitoring alert shows the decline rate jumping from 2 percent to 40 percent. Step 1, the on-call lead declares an incident and opens a shared channel. Step 2, the runbook says to route traffic back to the last known-good model version, which takes about 5 minutes. Step 3, if that version is also affected, the fallback switches to the rule-based checks that predate the model. Step 4, the team notifies customer support. Step 5, once stable, the team investigates the root cause in daylight and writes a review. For a regional outage, the DR plan might target an RTO of 60 minutes and an RPO of 15 minutes, meaning the copy of model artifacts and features must be no more than 15 minutes stale.

The common mistake is a plan that has never been tested, or a fallback that depends on the same component that just failed. A rollback to a model stored on the broken server is not a rollback.

In a running system, a missing fallback means that when the model fails, every payment is either blocked or approved blindly, and both outcomes harm customers and the business.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a model that reads supplier invoices and sends each one to the correct payables queue. At 09:30 the misroute rate climbs from 1 percent to 25 percent. Step 1: the on-call engineer declares an incident and opens a shared channel. Step 2: the runbook says to roll back to the previous model version, but that version is stored on the serving host that just failed, so the rollback cannot start because the host is unreachable. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the team tells the payables supervisors that some invoices may be delayed. Step 5: after recovery, the team writes a review. Which action best fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Switch to the manual payables review queue that predates the model, because the rollback target shares the failed component.
Retrain the classifier on the last week of invoices before restoring any routing.
Wait for the failed host to reboot before taking any further action, since no other version exists.
Retry the rollback against the same host every five minutes until it succeeds.
questions.why: A fallback must not depend on the component that just failed, so when the rollback target is on the broken host the team moves to the pre-model fallback, here the manual review queue.

questions.prompt: A billing-forecast team's plan sets a recovery point objective of 2 hours, but its model artifacts and features are copied to a backup site only once every 6 hours. Which statement is correct?
choices: The plan meets its recovery point objective, because that objective only measures how long the restore takes.
The plan cannot meet its recovery point objective, because up to 6 hours of changes could be lost in a failure.
The recovery point objective is about how long the restore takes, so the 6-hour copy interval has no bearing on it.
The plan meets its recovery point objective, because each copy is taken at the start of a 6-hour window and so is never stale.
questions.why: The recovery point objective is the most data, measured in time, that can be lost, and a copy every 6 hours can leave up to 6 hours of data missing, which exceeds the 2-hour limit.

questions.prompt: A dispatch-scheduling model has a recovery time objective of 4 hours. An outage begins at 08:00 and service is restored at 11:30. Which statement is true?
choices: The recovery time objective was missed, because restoration must always take the full four hours.
The recovery time objective was met only if the data loss was also under 4 hours.
The recovery time objective was met, since 3.5 hours is within the 4-hour limit.
The recovery time objective is not measured in hours, so the comparison cannot be made.
questions.why: The recovery time objective is the longest acceptable time to be back up, and restoration at 11:30 after an 08:00 start is 3.5 hours, which is inside the 4-hour limit.

questions.prompt: A pricing team wrote a rollback runbook two years ago and has never run it. Which risk matters most?
choices: The runbook is safe as long as the pricing model has not changed, since rollbacks never depend on context.
The plan has not been proven: an untested rollback may fail at 2 a.m. when the on-call person relies on it.
The main risk is only the cost of storing the document.
Runbooks cannot be stored as written text, so the plan is invalid.
questions.why: A plan that has never been tested is a common failure point, because its steps and fallbacks may not work under the pressure of a real incident.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a production AI service what a contingency plan covers, how incident response differs from disaster recovery, and one tradeoff or limit in the recovery targets the team agrees on.
lessons.modelAnswer: A contingency plan covers what we do when the AI service misbehaves or fails. Incident response is the fast, short-term part: detect the problem, contain it, usually by rolling back to a known-good model or switching to a simpler fallback, communicate, then find the root cause afterwards. Disaster recovery is the larger rebuild after a major loss, such as a lost region or corrupted data store, and it is judged by two targets. The recovery time objective is how long we can be down, and the recovery point objective is how much recent data we can lose. The tradeoff is cost: a tighter RPO usually means continuous replication, which costs more and adds complexity, so we set targets the business has accepted, not the lowest possible numbers. We also have to test the plan, because an untested fallback is a guess.
rubricPoints: Incident response is about fast detection, containment, and a rollback or fallback under a runbook
Disaster recovery restores service after a major loss and is judged by RTO and RPO
Recovery targets involve a cost or complexity tradeoff and must be agreed with the business
The fallback must not depend on the failed component, and the plan must be tested

suggested.rationale: A planned disaster-recovery planner would let the learner set RTO and RPO targets and check whether a recovery design meets them, which this objective needs.

scenarios.title: Triage model for insurance claims at Brightwater Health Plans
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Health Plans is a fictional health insurer. Its team is building a machine learning model, meaning software that learns patterns from past examples to make predictions, that scores incoming claims so that likely straightforward claims get fast-tracked and complex ones go to human adjusters. The project manager, Dana, has been asked to support the responsible and trustworthy AI effort. The training data holds past claims with PII (personally identifiable information, meaning any data that can identify a person, such as names, dates of birth, and member ID numbers). The model was trained on claims from the last six years, and early tests show that claims from one postal region are flagged for manual review far more often than others, even though the region's claims are similar in complexity. Legal wants a record of who approved what before the model goes live, and a state regulator has asked how the model reaches its decisions. Dana must respond to the following:

1. Name the privacy practice Dana should oversee before the training data is used again, and explain what it protects against.
2. Name the specific bias check that would reveal the regional pattern, and describe how Dana would confirm whether the pattern is unfair or justified.
3. Describe what Dana should document about the model's selection and data sources so that the regulator and internal stakeholders can understand how it works.
4. Describe the accountability records Dana should keep so that every version of the model and its training data can be traced and approved.
subParts: Privacy practice before reuse of training data
Specific bias check for the regional pattern
Transparency documentation for regulator and stakeholders
modelAnswer: Dana should oversee a privacy impact assessment, which is a structured review, done before the data is used, that maps what personal data is collected, why it is needed, who can access it, and what harm could follow a leak or misuse. Alongside it she should confirm PII governance protocols: rules that say which identifying fields are removed, masked, or replaced with codes before training, and that the data is encrypted at rest and in transit with access limited to named roles. This protects members from having their identities exposed through the model or the training files, and it limits who can see raw records. A common mistake is assuming that removing names alone makes data anonymous, when dates of birth and postal regions together can still identify people. If this is skipped, a data exposure can trigger legal penalties and loss of trust even if the model itself performs well.

The specific check is a demographic representation and fairness test: Dana would compare the rate at which the model flags claims for manual review across postal regions, and ideally across other groups the company is permitted to analyse, such as age bands. Representation analysis asks whether each group is fairly present in the training data, while fairness testing asks whether outcomes differ for groups with similar claim complexity. To judge whether the gap is unfair or justified, Dana would control for legitimate factors such as claim type and cost, then check whether the gap disappears or persists. If it persists without a valid reason, a bias-mitigation technique, such as rebalancing the training data, adjusting the decision threshold for that group, or removing a proxy feature that stands in for region, would be tested and re-measured. A common mistake is checking only overall accuracy, which can look high while one group is treated worse. If unaddressed, the company could be sending some members to slower review for reasons unrelated to their claims.

Dana should document the model-selection rationale: why this model type was chosen over simpler alternatives, what accuracy and fairness trade-offs were weighed, and who approved the choice. She should also document data-source reporting: where each training field came from, the time period covered, known gaps, and how PII was treated. For explainability, she should record the factors that most influence a flag, written in plain language that adjusters and the regulator can follow, along with any limits of the explanation. This lets outside reviewers verify how decisions are reached. A common mistake is writing documentation only for the data science team in technical terms, which leaves regulators and frontline staff unable to check or challenge decisions. If the documentation is weak, the company may be unable to answer a regulator's question about a specific denial or flag.

Dana should maintain version control, a system that gives each model, dataset, and training run a unique identifier and records what changed between versions, so that any past model can be reconstructed. She should keep an audit trail, a time-stamped log of who did what, including stakeholder approval records showing that legal, the clinical lead, and the business owner signed off on each release, with the reasons attached. This makes it possible to explain which model made a given decision and who authorised its use. A common mistake is updating the model or retraining on new data without logging the change, so that the version in production cannot be matched to its approval. If that happens, the company cannot prove compliance during an audit and may have to pause the system until the gap is closed.

scenarios.title: Harrowgate Parcels: Late-Delivery Prediction Tool Business Case
scenarios.scenario: Harrowgate Parcels is a fictional regional delivery company with about 400 drivers and three depots. Its operations director, Mira Solberg, wants an AI tool that predicts which parcels are likely to miss their delivery window, so dispatchers can reassign them early. A subject matter expert (SME), meaning a frontline person who knows the work well, has confirmed the problem is real. The steering group will decide on funding next week, and you are the project lead who must prepare the pack. Total cost of ownership (TCO) means every cost of the tool across its whole life, not only the build. Return on investment (ROI) is the net gain divided by the total cost, shown as a percentage. The sponsor's draft says the tool 'will save millions', but no figures back that up. The current figures are: a one-time build cost of 180,000; cloud and data costs of 45,000 per year; ongoing staff upkeep of 60,000 per year; and dispatcher training of 25,000 once. Missed-window penalties now cost about 1,200,000 per year, and the vendor's pilot suggested a 15 percent reduction, which the team has not yet verified. Complete the following for the steering group: 1. Build a three-year TCO and a simple ROI for the proposal, and state how sensitive the answer is to the 15 percent assumption. 2. Name two failure modes of the prediction tool, one of which is an ethical or fairness risk for drivers, and give a mitigation for each. 3. Draft the scope statement: list in-scope and out-of-scope functions, and propose two key performance indicators (KPIs), with a performance threshold for each.
subParts: Three-year TCO and ROI with sensitivity
Two failure modes with mitigations, including one ethics risk
Scope statement with in/out items and two KPIs
modelAnswer: TCO over three years is the build 180,000 plus cloud and data 135,000 (45,000 times 3) plus staff upkeep 180,000 (60,000 times 3) plus training 25,000, which totals 520,000. Benefits at the claimed 15 percent reduction are 180,000 per year (15 percent of 1,200,000), or 540,000 over three years. Net gain is 540,000 minus 520,000, which is 20,000. ROI is net gain divided by total cost, so 20,000 divided by 520,000, about 3.8 percent over three years. The answer is highly sensitive: at 10 percent reduction, benefits fall to 360,000 and the project loses about 160,000; at 20 percent, benefits rise to 720,000 and net gain is about 200,000. The steering group should see this range, should be told the 15 percent figure is unverified, and should be shown that year one benefits may be lower while the tool ramps up. A plain statement that the case is marginal at the claimed rate and depends on verifying the reduction is the correct conclusion, not an unqualified saving of millions.

Failure mode one: the model's predictions are wrong for a depot or route that differs from the pilot data, so dispatchers reassign parcels that would have arrived on time, wasting driver hours. Mitigation: validate accuracy per depot before rollout and keep a human dispatcher approval step. Failure mode two, the ethics risk: the model flags certain drivers' routes as high-risk because they cover harder areas, and managers then judge those drivers unfairly, which can affect pay and ratings. Mitigation: check whether prediction error or flag rates differ across route types or driver groups, restrict the tool's output to parcel reassignment rather than individual driver scoring, and set a review process for any driver-level use.

In scope: predicting likely late parcels for the three depots, showing a flag to dispatchers, and logging each reassignment decision. Out of scope: scoring or ranking individual drivers, changing pay or ratings, routing optimisation for vehicles, and any customer-facing notifications. Two KPIs with thresholds: first, the share of predicted late parcels that actually miss their window, with a threshold of at least 70 percent precision during the four-week pilot; second, the reduction in missed-window penalties measured against the prior twelve-month baseline, with a threshold of at least 10 percent within six months of rollout. If either threshold is missed, the steering group reviews the project before further funding.

scenarios.title: Late Shipment Prediction: Is the Data Ready?
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Logistics is a fictional regional freight company. It wants an AI model that flags shipments likely to arrive late, so dispatchers can reroute them before the delay happens. Dana, the new project manager, has been handed a data pipeline with three sources: the internal shipment database covering the last four years, a legacy archive of scanned delivery logs from two regions acquired in 2019, and a commercial weather feed bought from an outside provider. Driver records in the shipment system include full names and home postcodes. Before the modelling team starts, Dana must work through these tasks:

1. Define the required data for flagging late shipments. List the data types and formats needed, roughly how many records are required, and the quality standard each key field must meet to be useful.

2. Check privacy and access rights for the weather feed and the driver records. Say what must be confirmed or changed before either one is used for training.

3. Assess the shipment data for completeness, consistency, and accuracy, and identify any gaps or bias that could weaken the model. Name at least one exploratory check you would run first.

4. Write a short readiness statement for the operations director explaining whether the data can support the model, using business terms rather than technical jargon.
subParts: Define required data types, volume, and quality standards
Check privacy and licence access for weather feed and driver records
Assess completeness, consistency, accuracy, and bias or gaps
Write a business-language readiness statement for leadership
modelAnswer: Required data is one row per completed shipment, held in structured tables. Key fields are origin depot code, destination, scheduled arrival time, actual arrival time, carrier, vehicle type, package weight, route ID, and date. Timestamps must be in one agreed time zone and stored as proper date-time values, not free text. Volume should be enough that each depot, season, and carrier appears many times, so tens of thousands of completed shipments is a reasonable starting point. The target label is whether actual arrival exceeded scheduled arrival by a threshold agreed with dispatch. Quality standards: the arrival-time fields should be complete for at least 98 percent of rows, the late label must follow one stated definition, and depot codes must match a single reference list. Each requirement is tied to the business goal of reducing late deliveries, so every field must be justified by how it helps predict lateness.

Weather feed: check the provider contract to confirm that using the data to train an internal model and to make predictions is permitted, whether results can be stored or shared, and whether the subscription covers all the regions needed. Driver records: these are personal data under data protection rules. Remove names and exact home postcodes, replace them with pseudonymous driver IDs, confirm the lawful basis for using the data and a retention limit, and restrict access to named staff. Get privacy or legal sign-off and record it. Do not begin training on raw personal fields, even temporarily. Until licence and privacy checks are signed off, these two sources should be treated as not yet usable.

Completeness: count missing values per field, noting in particular any gaps in actual arrival times, since the label depends on them. Consistency: check that depot codes are spelled the same way across systems, because the legacy archive uses older codes that must be mapped to current ones. Accuracy: sample about 200 records and compare them against signed delivery receipts to estimate how often the stored values are wrong. Bias and gaps: the 2019 acquired regions may be sparsely represented or recorded differently, so a model could be less reliable there; compare late-delivery rates and record counts by region and carrier to see whether some groups are under-represented. Exploratory analysis: before modelling, plot the distribution of delay times and package weights and look for impossible values such as negative durations or weights of zero, which usually indicate entry errors.

The shipment history from the main regions is strong enough to support a first model, subject to fixing known gaps in the data. The weather feed can be used once its licence terms are confirmed in writing. Driver information can only be used in de-identified form, which needs privacy approval. The legacy regions need their codes mapped and records checked before they can be trusted, so the first model should be limited to the main regions and extended later. Leadership needs to decide two things: approve the weather licence and approve the de-identification approach. Timing and risks depend on those decisions. The model's eventual accuracy is not guaranteed by this assessment; it only shows the data is fit to begin.

scenarios.title: Late-Delivery Prediction Model Gate Review at Harbor Parcel Logistics
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Parcel Logistics is a fictional regional parcel carrier that wants to flag shipments likely to arrive late so dispatchers can reroute them early. You are the project manager. The team has a model in development. It is a supervised learning model, meaning it learns from past examples where the correct answer (here, whether a parcel arrived late) is already recorded. The data science lead, Priya, reports the following. The training table combines two years of shipment records. About 9 percent of rows have a blank in the pickup_scan_time column, and the team filled those blanks with the column average. The column delivery_exception_code is filled in only after a parcel is delivered, so it is populated for every late parcel. The data scientists tried two models. One is a gradient-boosted tree model, which builds many small decision trees one after another and combines them; it is often accurate but hard to explain. The other is a logistic regression model, which gives each input a single weight; it is simpler and easy to explain. The boosted trees scored best after the team adjusted hyperparameters, which are settings people choose before training starts, such as tree depth and learning rate. They chose those settings by checking scores on the same held-out test set (data kept aside for a final check) that they plan to report to the steering committee. No experiment log exists, and nobody has recorded which data version produced which result. The steering committee meets Thursday and must decide whether to approve the data for training now and, later, whether to approve the model for live use. Your tasks: 1. Decide whether the data passes the go/no-go gate for training, and name the specific problems you would require fixed before a go. 2. Recommend which model to carry forward, weighing complexity against interpretability, and state the evaluation method you would require before comparing the two fairly. 3. Explain what must be in place for the training and tuning to be reproducible and trustworthy, and state whether the current model is ready to be operationalized.
modelAnswer: The verdict is no-go for now. A go/no-go gate is a checkpoint where the team decides, against written criteria, whether data is good enough to start training. Three problems block a go. First, the blanks in pickup_scan_time: filling blanks with an average (called imputation, meaning replacing a missing value with an estimate) can be acceptable, but 9 percent of rows is a lot, and a missing scan may itself signal a real operational problem. The team should find out why scans are missing and record the rule used. Second, delivery_exception_code causes data leakage. Leakage means an input contains information that will not exist at the moment a prediction is needed. Worked example: the code 'LATE_HOLD' appears on 70 percent of late parcels in training, so the model looks excellent. In dispatch, the code is blank for every parcel when the prediction is needed, so the model's accuracy collapses. The column must be removed and the model rebuilt. Third, there is no dated, fixed data version, so the training set cannot be recreated. Gate criteria should be written down: missing values explained and handled by a recorded rule, no fields filled in after the outcome, and a named, dated data snapshot. Common mistake: approving training because the data is 'mostly fine'. Consequence: a model trained on this data reports inflated quality and would mislead dispatchers once live.

Supervised learning means the model learns a mapping from inputs to a labeled outcome. Choosing an algorithm is a tradeoff. Boosted trees often give higher accuracy on messy tabular data but are harder to explain. Logistic regression is simpler, quick to audit, and its weights show which factors push lateness risk up or down. The current comparison is not fair. The boosted-tree score was reached by tuning against the test set, so it is optimistic. A fair method is cross-validation on the training data only. Cross-validation means splitting training data into several folds, training on all but one fold, testing on the left-out fold, rotating through every fold, and averaging the results. Worked example: with five folds, logistic regression averages 0.78 accuracy and boosted trees average 0.83, each with a spread of about 0.02. The gap is real, but the team must also weigh whether a 5-point gain justifies losing explanations that dispatchers and auditors can follow. Recommendation: carry both forward, treat logistic regression as the baseline, and require the boosted model to beat it by a meaningful margin before it is chosen. The test set should be opened once, at the end, for a final score. Common mistake: tuning hyperparameters on the test set, which turns it into a second training set and inflates results. Consequence: choosing the boosted model on inflated numbers means approving a model that performs worse in live dispatch than the committee was told.

Reproducibility means someone else can rebuild the same result from the same inputs. Configuration management means recording exact versions of the data, code, software libraries, and settings used for each run. Experiment tracking means logging every training run with its data version, hyperparameters, cross-validation scores, and date. Peer review of model design means an independent expert checks the approach before approval. Worked example: run 14 scored 0.84, but there is no record of which data snapshot or tree depth produced it. When the data is refreshed, nobody can say whether a score drop came from the model or the data. The fix is to give each run an ID linked to a named data snapshot, a saved settings file, and its scores, and to lock the test set so it is opened only once. Readiness for operationalization: the model is not ready. Before approval it needs the leakage column removed and the model retrained, every run tracked and reproducible, an independent peer review of the design, a drift monitoring plan (drift means real-world data slowly changing so the model's accuracy falls), and a rollback plan for returning to the previous approach. Common mistake: treating a strong test score as proof of readiness. Consequence: without monitoring, a model can lose accuracy for months while dispatchers keep trusting its flags.

scenarios.title: Claims Triage Model Go-Live at Larkspur Insurance
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Insurance Co. is a fictional regional car insurer. Its data science team has built a model that reads incoming auto claim forms and sorts each claim into either a fast-track queue or a standard-review queue. The model has passed evaluation and is ready for production, meaning it is approved to make live routing decisions rather than run quietly in the background. You are the project manager, and go-live is six weeks away.

Some terms first. A rollback is a planned way to return a live system to the last known good version when a new release misbehaves. A model version is a saved, labelled copy of a trained model, so you can say exactly which one is running. Drift is a gradual change in the data a model sees after launch compared with the data it learned from, so its accuracy can fall even though no code changed. A KPI, or key performance indicator, is a measurable number the business uses to judge success, here the share of claims routed correctly. An adjuster is the staff member who reviews a claim and decides on payment. Production support is the team that keeps the live system running after the project team leaves.

Worked example of drift: the training data had 12 percent of claims involving collisions with driver-assist cameras. Six months after launch that share rises to 31 percent, because a popular new vehicle model has these cameras. The model saw few such claims in training, so its fast-track error rate climbs from 3 percent to 9 percent over two months. A monitor that compares the weekly input mix against the training mix, and raises an alert when any major category moves more than 10 percentage points, would have flagged the shift in the first week.

Common mistake: treating the rollback as optional, or planning to work it out during an outage. Consequence: if the new release sends claims to the wrong queue and no rollback has been rehearsed, adjusters may approve or deny claims wrongly for hours while the team searches for the previous model file.

Your tasks:
1. Write the rollback trigger and steps for this deployment. Name who decides and how quickly the previous version must return to service.
2. Define the drift monitor for the claims model, including its alert threshold, and say what action follows an alert.
3. Describe the handover to the production support team, and list what the final lessons-learned report must contain.
subParts: Rollback trigger, decision owner, and restore steps
Drift monitor design, alert threshold, and follow-up action
Handover to production support and lessons-learned contents
modelAnswer: The trigger is a fast-track error rate above 5 percent over any rolling 24-hour window, or any claim found in a sampled audit to have been routed to the wrong queue. The claims operations lead makes the rollback call within 15 minutes of the alert. The steps are: point live routing back to the previous model version (for example version 2.3) stored in the model registry, which is the saved catalogue of versions; confirm the restored version with a set of known test claims; send all incoming claims to standard review while the switch completes; notify adjusters that the fast-track queue is paused; and record the incident with timestamps. The target is restoring service within 30 minutes. The rollback must be rehearsed in a test environment before go-live, and the previous version must be kept deployable with its files checked, not deleted after release.

The drift monitor runs weekly. It compares the share of each major claim category in live inputs against the share in the training data, and it tracks the error rate on a sample of claims that adjusters review by hand. The alert fires if any major category shifts by more than 10 percentage points from its training share, or if the fast-track error rate passes 5 percent. When an alert fires, the data science team reviews the cause within two business days and recommends one of three actions: retrain the model on recent data, adjust the threshold, or temporarily send more claims to human review. Each alert and its decision is logged so that the pattern is visible over time.

The handover package goes to production support before the project team steps back. It includes a runbook, which is a step-by-step operating guide; named owners for each duty; an on-call rota, meaning who answers alerts at each hour; the dashboards and KPI definitions; the model version history; the monitoring thresholds; the rollback procedure; and a list of known limitations, such as weak performance on the driver-assist collision pattern. Production support should shadow the live system for two weeks before taking primary responsibility. The final lessons-learned report should cover what went well and what did not, the drift findings and how they were handled, KPI results against the pre-launch baseline, open risks with owners, and formal sign-off by the business owner.
